title: 3-Point Stance: How Drake Maye can bounce back from his rough start
summary: Two games into the 2026 season, Drake Maye has not looked like himself. So far, the New England Patriots quarterback has thrown four interceptions to just one touchdown. Maye committed three of those turnovers in the fourth quarter alone against the Seattle Seahawks, effectively losing New England the season opener. While the 2025 MVP runner-up’s […]
full_text: Two games into the 2026 season, Drake Maye has not looked like himself. So far, the New England Patriots quarterback has thrown four interceptions to just one touchdown. Maye committed three of those turnovers in the fourth quarter alone against the Seattle Seahawks, effectively losing New England the season opener. While the 2025 MVP runner-up’s third season hasn’t been catastrophic by any means and doesn’t warrant long-term concern, he consistently appears to be flustered in the pocket and not confident in what he’s seeing past his offensive line. And considering the Patriots soon match up against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Buffalo Bills and the Chicago Bears before star wide receiver A.J. Brown can return, timely adjustments need to be made. Although we can’t know exactly how Maye is processing the field, we have the resources to make estimates about why the signal-caller has struggled and how he can respond. Embracing the short game It’s important to note that NFL defenses are always adjusting. Therefore, Maye will have to adapt while also reestablishing the traits that made him an MVP candidate just one season ago. Across the Patriots’ first two contests, the Seahawks and Pittsburgh Steelers defenses lined up with two-high safeties just over 50% of the time when facing Maye. Oftentimes, their play designs call for split-safety coverage, with their defense playing in cover two, four, or the dreaded cover six. Progressing past the chains by taking the routine underneath plays forces those safeties to eventually adapt and play closer to the line of scrimmage. Excelling in the short passing game involves remaining “disciplined,” a word offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels used last week to describe how New England can adjust to how opposing teams will approach defending Maye. The 24-year-old was efficient in that approach against Seattle, leading the reigning Super Bowl champions 7-0 at halftime, until he “lost patience.” McDaniels added that there’s a “fine line” between taking care of the ball and taking what the defense allows while staying aggressive and making downfield plays. He called that attribute one of Maye’s greatest. Reestablishing his poise in the pocket Maye’s presence in the pocket is an area where the third-year quarterback has struggled to start the season, lacking the poise and composure that allowed him to methodically maneuver around pressure and throw with strong velocity and accuracy while staying in the pocket. Yet this season, Maye often bails from the pocket when he doesn’t need to. He appears to be playing too quickly, second-guessing himself and making abrupt decisions, potentially indicating that opposing defenses are speeding him up mentally as he diagnoses what’s happening in front of him. Pro Football Focus assigned Maye a 26.8 passing grade under pressure. A potential reason why he looks stiff in the pocket may be an effort to prevent fumbles, which he struggled with in the 2025 postseason, losing possession four times. Still, as McDaniels alluded to, there’s a middle ground. Recapturing those attributes begins with Maye playing more decisively without letting defenses accelerate his mental processing. That means operating the short passing game quickly and with confidence in his decision-making. “Being decisive and believing in what you see,” head coach Mike Vrabel said on Wednesday about his quarterback. “Again, what we ask all our players to do is prepare to try to play fast and aggressively and make great decisions. “Ultimately, it’s [Maye’s] responsibility to distribute the football as quickly and decisively as possible in the places that it’s supposed to go, continuing not to force things and try to just create a next play on every single play.” Preventing the underthrows If defenses are disrupting Maye’s timing, it could also be contributing to his uncharacteristic underthrows. Operating in the pocket while questioning decisions in the moment can alter his throwing mechanics and timing, causing passes to fall short. Two of Maye’s takeaways resulted from passes coming up short, with the final one against the Seahawks being an ill-advised decision to force a pass rather than settle for a tying field-goal attempt. That trend could make Sunday’s matchup especially challenging as Jacksonville’s defense excels at producing turnovers. Last season, the Jaguars ranked No. 2 in the NFL with 22 total interceptions, which was just one takeaway shy of the Bears in first. Throughout their two games thus far, they already have two. Until Maye makes the necessary adjustment, the Patriots could be playing from behind on Sunday. “One of the best things about getting new chances every week is having to let the other ones go,” Maye said on Wednesday. “That’s one of the best things about this sport and playing this position. You have to let plays go, and you want to be attacking the next play, learning from the ones in the past and getting after the next one. “So, I definitely think [it’s] hard to play this position when you’re thinking about a lot of different things. It’s going to be natural to think about motions, fronts, defenses, what our guys are doing, route concepts and what they’re doing versus the play we have [set] up. So, just thinking and trying to be instinctive. That’s one of the best things I learned in college is to be instinctive and try to play as fast as you can back there.”
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Defensive head-to-head preview: Saints vs Raiders
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are entering the Superdome with a 2-0 record under new head coach Klint Kubiak. And while Kubiak is known for being one of the better offensive play-callers in the NFL, it’s actually been the defense for Vegas that has been leading the charge through the first two weeks. The Raiders come […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints safety Jonas Sanker (7) and New Orleans Saints defensive end Chase Young (99) wait for the play during a regular season NFL football game between the New Orleans Saints and the Detroit Lions on September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are entering the Superdome with a 2-0 record under new head coach Klint Kubiak. And while Kubiak is known for being one of the better offensive play-callers in the NFL, it’s actually been the defense for Vegas that has been leading the charge through the first two weeks. The Raiders come into Week 3 leading the NFL with 8 sacks and a 50% pressure rate, all while only blitzing 7.4% of the time. The Raiders are showing that they are going to get pressure with four, and when they do, they are going to get home and finish the job with a sack. The Raiders have been able to do this because they have transitioned from a 4-3 defense under former DC Patrick Graham to a 3-4 defense under new DC Rob Leonard. The simulated pressure looks force QBs to hold the ball longer after the snap because the pre-snap protection could have identified the incorrect pass protection. The Raiders are not only getting sacks without heavy blitz packages, but they are also forcing turnovers. The Raiders have 3 interceptions through two games, which has them tied for second across the league, and they are also +2 in turnover margin. They have also been able to hold teams to 23.5 points per game. But while their passing defense has been really solid, the run defense is middle of the pack. The Raiders are giving up just over 100 rushing yards per game, which has them ranked 16th in the league. This game has an obvious key to victory for the New Orleans Saints: Can they hold up on the offensive line, especially with Kelvin Banks Jr. not playing for a while? If they can manage the protection and establish a rushing attack, it will help expose the defense and give Tyler Shough the ability to make plays off play action. The Saints cannot allow the defense to pin its ears back and just attack the offense however it wants to. Also, keep in mind the level of competition that the Raiders have faced over the past two weeks. They matched up against the Chargers and Dolphins, who may very well be two of the worst teams in the league. As for the Saints, the defense has been better than what the numbers are showing. The Saints’ defensive performance against the Lions may have been an outlier to begin the season. Last year under DC Brandon Staley, the Saints were a top-10 defense in the NFL, and in Week 1 they gave up a lot of yards on the ground. But in Week 2, against one of the most prolific rushing combinations in the league, they held the Ravens to 108 rushing yards and 312 yards of total offense. The Saints defense is showing so far that its ability to defend the pass is starting to take another step forward, while the run defense still needs a little more consistency. The question becomes: Which run defense shows up? Ashton Jeanty has not had a great start to the season. So far, he has 150 yards on 44 carries and 0 TDs through two games. He’s averaging 3.4 yards per carry, while the Saints are allowing 5.0 yards per carry through two weeks. It is very important for the Saints to stop Jeanty early and keep the Raiders offense off schedule. Cousins, being the veteran QB he is, needs to stay ahead of the chains to keep the offense moving. He is not a dynamic QB, but if the offense is steady enough and he is in the game late, he can make the throws necessary to threaten the Saints and potentially win this game on the road. Forcing the Raiders into second-and-long and third-and-long situations will be very important. If you look at this Raiders offense, it almost resembles a lesser-quality version of the Detroit Lions. Cousins is similar to Goff in that both like to get rid of the ball quickly and are statues in the pocket. Both offenses feature a dynamic running back with the ability to break a game open in Jeanty and Gibbs. They also have an all-around TE who must be identified on every play—a good blocker and elite pass catcher—with Bowers for the Raiders and LaPorta for the Lions. The comparisons are there, but the difference is that the Lions have better talent at some of the core positions, and the Saints nearly stole that game on the road. Being at home and having the defense get a chance to play with this crowd behind it should be a huge advantage, especially on third downs. This is one area where the defense has been very good so far this season. The Saints have held their first two opponents to 9-of-22 on third downs, a 40.9% conversion rate. Keep the running game in check, force them into third-and-long situations, and let the pass rush go to work with the decibels in the Dome touching 115-120. If the Saints can do that, this should be a great opportunity for the defense to have a strong outing. Which defense do you think has the advantage in this game? Were you surprised that the Raiders are leading the league in several defensive categories through the first two weeks?
author: Anthony Parker

title: College Players to Watch: Week 3
summary: Through the first two games, the Saints are showing signs of improvement in pass defense, but stopping the run is still a bit of an issue, as they are allowing an astounding 5.0 yards per carry. That’s an area that will need to be addressed in the offseason by adding additional personnel. It is only […]
full_text: BATON ROUGE, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 5: Ty Benefield #2 of the LSU Tigers celebrates after a play against the Clemson Tigers at Tiger Stadium on September 5, 2026 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by Ella Hall/University Images via Getty Images} Through the first two games, the Saints are showing signs of improvement in pass defense, but stopping the run is still a bit of an issue, as they are allowing an astounding 5.0 yards per carry. That’s an area that will need to be addressed in the offseason by adding additional personnel. It is only Week 3, so a lot of things can change. Here are some players to watch in college football with a great slate of games on Saturday. Justin Scott, a defensive lineman from Miami, is a 6’4”, 303-pound interior lineman who, for his size, is unbelievably quick. He has a really great first step and was an anchor for the Miami defense that helped lead the Hurricanes to the 2025 national championship. So far this season, Scott has 5 total tackles and a PFF grade of 70. Miami will face Central Michigan at 5:30 p.m. on The CW. Another defensive lineman to watch this week will be Will Echoles from Ole Miss. Coming off an absolutely dominant performance against LSU last week, it will be fun to watch how he follows it up against a gritty, run-heavy Florida team. Echoles is currently ranked as a top-15 player on the big board and is widely considered to be the first interior defensive lineman who could be drafted. Ole Miss finds itself as the underdog as the Rebels/Landsharks/Black Bears travel to Gainesville for a 2:30 p.m. kickoff on ABC. Another big performance from Echoles will be needed to help keep their undefeated season intact. Finally, A’mauri Washington is a name to watch. He is currently trending up big boards and is the No. 21-ranked player. Washington is another interior defensive lineman who plays for the University of Oregon. Washington does not have the flashy stats, but the athleticism is off the charts. This is a 6’3”, 303-pound lineman who can run 21 miles per hour, squat 755 pounds and bench press 475 pounds. Washington has the physical ability, but he is still a prospect who will need to showcase continued development as the season progresses. Oregon is on the road in a major Big Ten matchup against USC. If the Ducks lose this game, their playoff hopes could be over. This game is set for a 6:30 p.m. kickoff on NBC. Who are some players you are excited to watch this weekend, and through two games, what areas would you like to see the Saints improve throughout the season? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: 5 questions about the Titans: Are ex-Giants paying off for Tennessee?
summary: There is, of course, a ton of familiarity between the New York Giants and Tennessee Titans. To learn even more about the Titans, we check in this week with Jimmy Morris of Music City Miracles for our weekly ‘5 questions’ segement. Ed: Assess the job that Brian Daboll has done thus far with the Tennessee […]
full_text: Wan’Dale Robinson | Getty Images There is, of course, a ton of familiarity between the New York Giants and Tennessee Titans. To learn even more about the Titans, we check in this week with Jimmy Morris of Music City Miracles for our weekly ‘5 questions’ segement. Ed: Assess the job that Brian Daboll has done thus far with the Tennessee offense. Does he look like the right offensive coordinator to help Cam Ward reach whatever his ceiling is? Getting Brian Daboll was huge for Robert Saleh. Reports suggest he wanted to trade up for Cam Ward in the 2025 draft, making it an exciting pairing. He called a really good game against the Eagles, with the exception of one play . As you were probably alluding to with your question, we don’t yet know Cam’s ceiling. For now, this offense is going to have to rely on a run game to move the football. They did a good job of balance in Week 2. As the season progresses, we will get a better idea of how good Daboll really is. Cam has two major issues that are hindering him right now. The first is his tendency to leave a clean pocket. That’s partially a result of the offensive line being so bad last season. Cam spent most of the season running for his life. The offensive line has been better through the first two games. A lot of the pressure Cam has faced has been self-induced. His second issue is his footwork when he throws the ball. He has the tendency to not set his feet when he throws, which causes inaccurate throws. That was supposed to be a big point of emphasis through the offseason. He hasn’t been any better at that in the two games. Hopefully, that is something that Daboll can coach him through this season. Ed: There are four Giants players who signed free agent contracts with the Titans. Can you give us a synopsis of each player’s role, and how he has performed? Jimmy: Austin Schlottman Schlottman has been solid so far. His familiarity with the system and the offensive line coach has been an asset to the team. Wan’Dale Robinson Robinson hasn’t gotten going yet, with only 6 catches for 47 yards in the first two games. Some of that is a product of Cam Ward’s struggles. The Titans need to get him more involved. Daniel Bellinger Bellinger has done a good job blocking in the run game. He only has 1 catch for 7 yards, but the Titans didn’t bring him in to be a threat in the passing game. Cor’Dale Flott Flott was terrible in the preseason. He missed last week’s game with a quad injury. He should be back this week, and they need him because the secondary hasn’t been very good. Ed: The Titans have, obviously, already taken several former Giants. If you could take one player off the current Giants roster and put him in the Titans’ lineup, who would it be? Why? Jimmy: This one is close between Malik Nabers and Brian Burns, but the Titans finally have a solid receiver room, so I will go with Burns. The Titans have been searching for an impact edge rusher since the Obama administration. Pairing Burns with Jeffery Simmons would give Tennessee one of the best pass rushes in the league and could hide the holes in the secondary. Ed: Tennessee went from looking horrible against the Jets to almost beating a good Eagles team. What was the difference, and is it sustainable? Jimmy: The biggest difference was that they forced two turnovers against the Eagles. The offense also did a better job of staying balanced. The Titans haven’t sustained any time of success in about 4 years, but last week’s game plan, especially on offense, gives me some hope that they are finally starting to move in the right direction. Ed: The Titans will be the underdogs on Sunday. Why can they win? On the flip side, why could they lose? Jimmy: They can win the game if they find success in the run game and force Jameis Winston into a couple of turnovers. This offense needs a short field or two if they are going to put up a lot of points. They could lose if Winston is able to hit a couple of big plays early. That would force them to go pass-heavy on offense, and that is not the recipe for them to have success right now.

title: NY Giants add backup QB to roster ahead of game vs. Tennessee Titans
summary: The New York Giants have signed veteran quarterback Jake Haener from their practice squad. Haener fills the 53-man roster spot vacated when Jaxson Dart was placed on injured reserve. The Giants also elevated wide receiver/kick returner Braxton Berrios and linebacker Malik Harrison from the practice squad for Sunday’s game against the Tennessee Titans. That is […]
full_text: Jake Haener | Getty Images The New York Giants have signed veteran quarterback Jake Haener from their practice squad. Haener fills the 53-man roster spot vacated when Jaxson Dart was placed on injured reserve. The Giants also elevated wide receiver/kick returner Braxton Berrios and linebacker Malik Harrison from the practice squad for Sunday’s game against the Tennessee Titans. That is the third and final elevation for each player. They will now have to be signed to the 53-man roster, or the Giants risk losing them. Haener has been in the league since 2023. His only game action came in 2024, when he played eight games with one start for the New Orleans Saints. He completed 18 of 39 passes with a touchdown and an interception. The Giants will start Jameis Winston at quarterback on Sunday. Winston was recently given a two-year, $13 million contract extension. Multiple reports have indicated that the Giants could sign a third quarterback as soon as Monday. The question will be who. Winston’s performance on Sunday could be a factor in how aggressive the Giants are in bringing in a third quarterback. There have been reports that they have reached out to veteran quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo, a free agent. it has also been reported that GM Joe Schoen has been working the phones to see if there is a trade to be made.

title: NFL Week 3 betting advice: Giants-Titans picks and props
summary: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 3 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! The Giants come home on Sunday licking (and nursing) their wounds after what can […]
full_text: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 3 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! The Giants come home on Sunday licking (and nursing) their wounds after what can only be described as a very sad few days in Los Angeles. The euphoria of the huge opening day win over Dallas quickly gave way to the reality that the team’s young franchise quarterback is lost for the remainder of the regular season. Not only must the team soldier on without Jaxson Dart, but a critical year of on-field development with the new coaching staff will be lost. No team or fan base experienced a bigger emotional swing over the first two weeks of this season than Big Blue and its great fans. I won’t belabor what happened on Monday night, other than to note that the season isn’t over. There’s a lot of football left to play for John Harbaugh’s team. Jameis Winston takes over for Dart, and he’s one of the more capable and experienced backups in the league. There’s some good news for the Giants. Their Week 3 opponent is the 0-2 Tennessee Titans, who had the first and fourth overall draft picks in 2025 and 2026 – meaning they’ve been even worse than the Giants, who had the third and sixth picks in those same drafts. The Titans fought hard against the Eagles at home last week in brutally hot conditions, only to lose the game on the final drive. A different kind of weather issue will greet the Titans this week. Steady rain and gusty wind is expected throughout the game on Sunday, so it should be a low-scoring affair, and turnovers could decide the outcome. Winston is a gambler, and will need to play smarter than he did on Monday night. One interesting subplot: There are coaches on both sides with plenty of familiarity with the other team, including Titans’ OC Brian Daboll and Giants’ QB coach and passing game coordinator Brian Callahan. Both Brians — Daboll (2-8 at the time of his dismissal) and Callahan (1-5 at the time of his) were relieved of their Head Coaching duties during the season last year, by the team they’ll be facing on Sunday. I’m sure Daboll wants to hang as many points as he can on New York. After going 2-1 in Week 1, I crapped out last week, at 0-3. Two of my bets were linked to the Giants’ offense and the Dart injury sealed my fate early. The line for the game is Giants -2.5, and the game total of 38.5 is the lowest on the board this week. The line moved four points on the Dart injury news, and the total surely reflects the dismal weather forecast. Let’s get to this week’s picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel and are as of Saturday, September 26. Giants – 2.5 (-114) . I think the Giants will be fired up, and will do enough to get the win in front of a soaked but enthusiastic home crowd. I also think the Titans aren’t a very good team, and should be getting at least a field goal from just about every other NFL team and especially on the road. Even with the injuries to Dart, the secondary, and edge defender Brian Burns, I think Big Blue still has a roster edge. The weather, and Winston’s penchant for mistakes, scare me a little, but I’m OK laying less than a field goal to this team. Cam Skattebo OVER 57.5 rushing yards (-114). New York will surely try to establish the run, and stick with it given the weather. The Titans are allowing 120 rushing yards per game, which is in the bottom half of the league. I expect New York to have something in the neighborhood of 30 rushing attempts (if not more), and Skat to get to this total, even with him sharing touches. Cam Ward UNDER 187.5 passing yards (-114). I’m sure the Titans will also try to pound the ball. This total would be normal for Ward in good weather – he averages slightly less than 185 passing yards per start for his career. The Giants’ secondary is banged up, and they’ll probably be without Brian Burns. No matter – this is a big number for Ward in bad weather. Those are the picks for Week 3. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 3 fantasy preview, with start/sit advice and more, right here.

title: College football Week 4: 2027 NFL Draft prospects for the NY Giants
summary: Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 4 of the 2026 College Football season! The Giants had their season turned upside down on Tuesday when it was revealed that quarterback Jaxson Dart would be lost for the season. That doesn’t change our focus for the Giants as we use the […]
full_text: South Carolina wide reciever Nyck Harbor catches a touchdown﻿ | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 4 of the 2026 College Football season! The Giants had their season turned upside down on Tuesday when it was revealed that quarterback Jaxson Dart would be lost for the season. That doesn’t change our focus for the Giants as we use the upcoming draft as a lens to evaluate the team — the Giants’ most pressing needs are still at “offensive weapon” (wide receiver, running back, or tight end), cornerback, and defensive tackle. However, it might adjust our frame of reference and force us to consider higher rated prospects who the Giants might not have been in position to draft with a healthy Dart. We’re not closing the door on a playoff push yet, but we’re aslo expanding the Giants’ potential draft window to more highly rated prospects. (14) Tennessee vs. (1) Texas ABC – noon Player highlight: Cam Coleman (WR, Texas) Arch Manning remains the player to watch on Texas’ roster. He’s vaulted back into the Top 5 conversation after leading a come-from-behind win over Ohio State back in Week 2. There’s no evidence that the Giants aren’t looking for a quarterback despite the injury to Jaxson Dart. The Giants might be interested in Texas’ offensive tackles, Trevor Goosby and Melvin Siani if Jermaine Eluemunor stumbles over the remainder of the season. That said, the Giants’ long-term need at wide receiver remains, and Cam Coleman could be a truly elite one. While Jeremiah Smith (WR, Ohio State) has been compared to Calvin Johnson or Julio Jones, Cam Coleman is much more in the “A.J. Green” mold as a receiver. He’s long, lean, and has elite body control and ball skills. He isn’t a burner down the field and will likely time in the 4.45-4.50 neighborhood. That said, his ability was obvious at Auburn (despite the state of their passing offense) prior to transferring to Texas, and he has the ability to emerge as a truly elite prospect. Texas’ roster is absolutely stacked with talent, but Coleman might be the best player regardless of position. Ideally, the Giants would have no chance at Coleman. However, the injury to Dart the the glut of talent in the 2027 draft could put him on the board for the Giants, so we should pay attention to him. (21) Florida vs. (4) Ole Miss ABC – 3:30 p.m. Player highlight: Jaden Baugh (RB, Forida) This is one of those games in which I’m cheating just a bit. This game actually features two excellent running backs in Florida’s Jaden Baugh and Kewan Lacy out of Ole Miss. The Giants could use more “juice” out of their backfield, and either one of these players would be an upgrade for the Giants’ backfield. The Giants love Cam Skattebo, with elite contact balance and the ability to consistently churn out 4 to 6 yards. However, Skattebo doesn’t have the long speed to pair with his explosiveness. Baugh has great size at 6-foot-1, 230 pounds with great vision, contact balance, and the speed to take advantage of glimmers of daylight. If there’s a whole in Baugh’s game and draft profile, it’s that he needs to show more in the passing game. That might be tough in a very limited Florida offense that runs through Baugh… On the ground. Lacy is a smaller back at 5-foot-9, 205 pounds, but runs with great toughness as well as agility and burst. He was running like a man possessed against Lane Kiffin’s LSU before suffering a painful shoulder injury. He led the SEC with 306 carries (1,567 yards, 5.1 per attempt) and 24 rushing touchdowns last year. Lacy has shown receiving upside with 29 receptions a year ago, but he’s also listed as questionable for this game. This promises to be an excellent game, and it’ll be fascinating to see if Trinidad Chambliss and Ole Miss can build on the momentum generated by their win over LSU. (8) Alabama vs. South Carolina ESPN – 7 p.m. Player highlight: Nyck Harbor, WR, South Carolina There are a number of ways we could go in this game. Alabama is once again talented, and South Carolina has a nice collection of future NFL players as well. Most scouts will be at the game for South Carolina quarterback LaNoriss Sellers and edge defender Dylan Stewart. Gamecocks’ cornerback Vicari Swain is another very intriguing name in light of the Giants’ thin secondary as well. However, we need to talk about SC receiver Nyck Harbor. There has never been a doubt about Harbor’s unreal athleticism, and the Olympic hopeful has headlined Bruce Feldman’s “Freaks List” three of the last four years. His absurd blend of size and speed can only be compared to that of Calvin Johnson… Except that Feldman himself opined on the McShay Show that Harbor is not only an inch and 10 pounds bigger than Johnson, he could be faster too. Feldman stated that where Megatron ran in the 4.3’s, Harbor could run in the 4.2’s despite being the size of many NFL tight ends. The problem is that Harbor has spent much of his college career aspiring to represent the USA as an Olympic track athlete, and has only recently fully committed himself to football. There are absolutely absurd flashes from Harbor, but he is still raw as a receiver and it shows. Going up against Alabama is Harbor’s best chance to make scouts around the NFL stand up and take notice of him as a football player, and not just an athlete. If he can have a good game against a sophisticated defense that’s stocked with future NFL players, he could see his draft stock rocket up and become a realistic option for the Giants if they’re looking to reinforce their receiving corps. Looking at the game as a whole, can South Carolina get back into the SEC race with a win over ‘Bama? (12) USC vs (20) Oregon NBC – 7:30 p.m. Player highlight: Bear Alexander (iDL, Oregon) As mentioned above, this is a great slate of games today, and I had to mention a second primetime game. This game has a bunch of context and subtext around it, largely related to the two quarterbacks. Oregon’s Dante Moore is still generally considered the top quarterback in the upcoming draft, however he hasn’t exactly taken the step expected of him after returning to school for the 2026 season. Conversely, USC QB Jayden Maiava is climbing draft boards as more people get a look at him. But that’s what national scouts will be interested in. We’re here for the Oregon defensive line, and their match-up against the USC offensive line and running game. USC is running the ball well with each of their top three running backs averaging over 5 yards per carry, while freshman Riley Wormley is averaging 7.3 yards per attempt (and 2 touchdowns) on 9 carries so far this year. They’ll be opposed by Bear Alexander and A’Mauri Washington. Alexander is a former top defensive line recruit who started his college career at Georgia, then transferred to USC before finally transferring to Oregon. He has a near prototypical frame at 6-foot-3, 310 pounds, and reportedly has 34-inch arms giving him great length to go with his mass. He’s a powerful defensive tackle who can attack and clog gaps as well as control blockers. Alexander is a pure power player who’s able to command double teams, overpower individual blockers and collapse the pocket. He’s much more of a run defender than a pass rusher, though he does have 5 passes defensed and 44 pressures coming into this year. I’ve previously talked about A’Mauri Washington, and he remains one of my favorite defensive tackles in the class. He strikes me as a classic “Giants” DT with a rare blend of size and athleticism, and both of these tackles have the potential to emerge as Top 50 talents.

full_text: WEEHAWKEN, NJ - SEPTEMBER 25: The sun sets on the skyline of midtown Manhattan, the Empire State Building and Hudson Yards as a rainbow forms ahead of an approaching nor'easter storm in New York City on September 25, 2026, as seen from Weehawken, New Jersey. (Photo by Gary Hershorn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The nor’easter expected to slam into the East Coast this weekend could have a major impact on Sunday’s New York Giants vs. Tennessee Titans game in East Rutherford, N.J. The National Weather Service is forecasting an inch or more of rain in the East Rutherford area on Saturday, followed by another half- to three-quarters of an inch of rain on Sunday. Temperatures are expected to be in the mid-60s, with steady winds around 20 MPH and gusts of up to 38 MPH. Sunday will mark Jameis Winston’s first start at quarterback for the Giants this season after the season-ending injury to Jaxson Dart. The wet, blustery conditions could make it a difficult day to throw, catch, kick, and hang on to the football. In John Harbaugh’s first season as head coach, the Giants have built a power running game that they will likely need to rely heavily upon Sunday afternoon. Conditions could also make travel to and from the game treacherous. If you are planning to attend, leave yourself extra time.

title: New York Giants mailbag: It’s all quarterback all the time
summary: Ed Helinski asks: What’s the Giants Plan C if Jameis Winston isn’t the answer for whatever reason? Ed says: Ed, how many times actually have a realistic Plan C at quarterback? The reality is that if you are down to your third quarterback, things are not going to go well. There are 32 NFL teams. […]
full_text: Ed Helinski asks: What’s the Giants Plan C if Jameis Winston isn’t the answer for whatever reason? Ed says: Ed, how many times actually have a realistic Plan C at quarterback? The reality is that if you are down to your third quarterback, things are not going to go well. There are 32 NFL teams. Even if every quarterback is healthy, there aren’t 32 good starting quarterbacks in the league. By extension, there aren’t 32 good backup quarterbacks. The truth is nobody ever wants to see their third quarterback play — that guy is a baseball cap-wearing third quarterback or practice squad guy for a reason. That said, I’m sure the Giants will look around at practice squads, a street free agent like Jimmy Garoppolo, and trade options. Considering how many quarterbacks have gotten hurt in the first two weeks of the season, though, how many teams are going to be willing to trade away someone they consider to be a capable backup? At this point, that’s GM malpractice. The Giants just gave Jameis Winston a two-year, $13 milliion extension. They didn’t do that to replace him as soon as they need a backup quarterback. Todd Graf asks: Do the OC and DC come down to the locker room at halftime or do they work the 2nd half game plan from the booth? Thought about this with Jameis taking over for Jaxson and his 1st half struggles…. And also because there isn’t much time at halftime. Ed says: Todd, let me clarify that to my knowledge defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson works from the sideline. To answer your question, all of the coaches who work from upstairs make a beeline for the locker room at halftime. At MetLife Stadium, that means taking the elevator from the sixth floor down to the ground floor and then hustling down the tunnel to the room for a brief interaction with John Harbaugh, players, and other coaches, then back upstairs before the second half starts. Ted Schwartz asks: All of the cards appeared to be aligning for what would be an exciting season where I finally could watch all of the games while being surrounded by fellow fans! Alas, the football gods have struck down that excitement. Watching the devastating injury to Dart and the massive blow it struck to this team for the season, leaves me wondering about accountability within the team. I know football is a dangerous sport and any player can get injured through no fault of their own or their teammates. But this injury appears to me to be squarely on the shoulders of the Left and Right tackle who both got beat badly on the same play and left their quarterback exposed to the vicious punishment his body received. Does this affect the team chemistry with some players feeling if even one of them did their job properly their quarterback would not be injured and the team would not be in this position. Dart stayed in the pocket, did not put himself unnecessarily in harms way and trusted and relied on his teammates, who failed him. Does the team discuss this as a whole, are the players spoken to individually, is there any penalty for them within the team environment or is it just chalked up as an unfortunate football injury. Have either of them spoken out about their role in this injury? Of course they didn’t mean for it to happen and Im sure they were trying their hardest not to let it happen. But they let their quarterback down, let their team down, and let their fans down. Ed says: Ted, trying to assign blame to other players for a guy getting injured is not constructive, and not something teams or players do. I did not get an opportunity to speak to Andrew Thomas or Jermaine Eluemunor when I was there on Wednesday. Both guys are among the best in the league at their jobs, and are highly-respected inside that locker room. Players get beat sometimes. The guys on the other side are also professionals. It happens. This “they let their quarterback down” stuff is way over the top. Spoken to individually? Penalty within the team? I am sure the team has looked at the film and understands why the play happened, but these guys aren’t children. I think you are looking for some type of team divide or finger-pointing that simply doesn’t exist. I think the video below from Chris Simms is instructive. I agree with him that this play was in “disarray” before the ball was snapped. That doesn’t mean I am blaming Dart, either. Dart’s not the first quarterback to get sandwiched by multiple defenders, and he won’t be the last. The play where Dart got hurt was in disarray before the snap. pic.twitter.com/b4WKB6p0wS — Chris Simms (@CSimmsQB) September 22, 2026 Bob Donnelly asks: How does the loss of Jaxson Dart impact your projection for Giant’s 2026 win/loss record? Ed says: Bob, as Big Blue View readers probably (should?) know I predicted 9-8, calling that the “most optimistic” prediction I could make for 2026. I would think 9-8 without Dart would be a fantastic season. I think right now it would be hard to complain about seven wins. The next three weeks — winnable games against the Titans, Cardinals, Commanders — will tell us more about what to expect. Patrick Morris asks: The injury to Jaxson Dart is awful. His play when he has been available has been inspiring. But, the season without him is not as hopeful, and the odds of the Giants having a high draft pick have gone up. If the Giants end the season with a poor record, but an opportunity to draft one of the top 3 QBs in the upcoming draft class…do they take it? Ed says: I don’t know what they would do. But, I think the answer would be no. My answer would definitely be no . John Urbielewicz asks: The inside linebacker play against the Rams was horrible. One could make an argument that Micah McFadden is our best inside linebacker at this time. I think Arvell Reese is going to be a great player in this league, but right now with Brian Burns missing time, I would move Arvell to the end rusher and play McFadden. Your thoughts? Ed says: John, no. Arvell Reese is an inside linebacker. That is what the Giants drafted him to be. That is where he has practiced since the spring. That is where he is best. The Giants align him outside occasionally to change the look of the defense and try to create desirable matchups. Maybe that happens a little more frequently with Burns out, but moving Reese to the edge and starting McFadden is an overreation. Chris Chianese asks: Ed, in your “Ride with Winston” article it left me thinking … finally there is someone showing some common sense and reality with the Dart injury and where we are with the QB for the Gs this season. First and foremost, Harbaugh and Schoen didn’t sign Winston to an extension to move on from him if Dart got injured. I suppose a person could take issue with Winston being the backup considering he is such a different QB than Dart. So, in other words, the Gs offense will need to be revamped to accommodate Winston’s abilities. So my question is, which QBs out there that are free agents or on a practice squad, most emulate what Dart’s abilities to sign as a backup to Winston? Milton? Hooker? Or, for continuity in the 2026 season, does signing Jimmy Garoppolo make more sense as a backup to Winston since Jimmy G is more like Winston? Ed says : Chris, I honestly don’t think emulating Dart has anything to do with it. I think the point is to find the player the Giants believe can do the best job helping them win games if he has to play. If that is a quarterback who offers the chance to use the quarterback run game, fine. If it is more of a pocket passer, fine. John Harbaugh has succeeded with Joe Flacco, a pocket passer, at quarterback. He also succeeded with a running quarterback — Lamar Jackson. Matt Nagy, Greg Roman, Brian Callahan have worked with both types. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: NY Giants news: Andrew Thomas to play, Jaxson Dart surgery, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants get ready to take on the Tennessee Titans tomorrow at 1 p.m. Giants’ season hinges on John Harbaugh after Jaxson Dart injury | The Athletic We’re going to learn a lot about the New York Giants over the next few […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants get ready to take on the Tennessee Titans tomorrow at 1 p.m. Giants’ season hinges on John Harbaugh after Jaxson Dart injury | The Athletic We’re going to learn a lot about the New York Giants over the next few weeks. The team was delivered a gut punch with the news that second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart is out for the season with a knee injury. But coach John Harbaugh didn’t get a $100 million contract just to captain the franchise through smooth seas. This type of adversity is when Harbaugh’s talents as a culture-building coach should emerge. Harbaugh isn’t a miracle worker. The Ravens went 6-12 in the 18 games they started a backup during the seven seasons since Lamar Jackson became their starter. The Giants don’t need a miracle, but they need Harbaugh’s leadership to prevent Dart’s injury from sending the season off the rails. Practicing what they preach John Harbaugh says the Giants had their best practice of the year yesterday and followed it up with a "very good" practice today pic.twitter.com/Cro3uKyVm2 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 25, 2026 Harbs Weekly: Turning the page to Tennessee | Giants.com Q: Like you said, the NFL is high-level drama. With everything that has transpired this week, are you just eager to get to Sunday and turn the page? Harbaugh: The guys are excited about the game. It’s an opportunity to get to 2-1, 1-0 for the week is the mantra. Circumstances are always what they are. So yeah, it’s a tough circumstance with the quarterback. It’s unique. We’re not the only team that’s ever faced that, not even the only team that’s facing it this week in the National Football League, and we won’t be the last team to face it. It’s not something that’s unknown to mankind. It’s an adversity that’s going to hopefully serve to make us a better football team and that’s really the goal – to become the best football team we can be. But within that, play our best football game this week and we have a team that’s really determined and really locked in to do that. Jaxson (Dart) is supporting that. He’s been in meetings all week supporting the guys and supporting Jameis (Winston). So yeah, we’re excited to play the game. NFL Week 3 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com The Giants’ offense will look different against the Titans. They’ll have to cater it to QB Jameis Winston’s skill set, which doesn’t include the same running ability as Jaxson Dart (knee). The Giants already have the plays in their playbook. Guard Jon Runyan said they have more than 300 plays already. Now, OC Matt Nagy & Co. will lean on what works better for Winston. That likely means using Winston’s arm and ability to throw downfield to complement the running game. Why are Giants barely putting Odell Beckham Jr. on the field?| New York Daily News Beckham and Jaxson Dart never appeared to develop any obvious chemistry during training camp, but Jameis Winston and Beckham had a rapport. They’re both veterans. Winston often plants his back foot and fires, and Beckham is a precise, timing-based route runner. And Beckham logged more snaps with the backups than the starters, giving him more time on task with Winston. And yet when Winston took over for Dart in Monday’s first quarter, and as the Giants’ offense floundered while falling behind big, Beckham was nailed to the bench. It just seems Beckham should be worked in as an option, particularly with Winston now under center. How Giants offense changes now with Jameis Winston at quarterback | The Record Cam Skattebo doesn’t see why anything has to change offensively for the New York Giants. With respect and love to Jaxson Dart, whom he called “my best friend” on the day the 23-year-old was placed on injured reserve with knee surgery pending, and Jameis Winston’s ascension to a starting role, Skattebo has a solution to replacing the juice missing without Dart. Giants trade candidate aims to spark ‘terrible’ defense: ‘It’s been hard’ | NJ.com The Giants need their defense to lift them in Sunday’s home game against the Titans — which still seems winnable, even without quarterback Jaxson Dart. But if coordinator Dennard Wilson’s group plays as poorly as it did Monday night in Los Angeles, the Giants are doomed — and coach John Harbaugh’s once-promising first season might begin to spiral out of control. On Sunday, they Giants will turn to a fascinating potential trade piece, outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux, since elite edge rusher Brian Burns will be sidelined by an ankle sprain he sustained in that 28-6 loss to the Rams. Special teams have been a bright spot The Giants have the best kickoff coverage unit through two weeks Average Drive Start Position After a Kickoff👇 pic.twitter.com/LjwOe03Wzg — Gridiron Stats and Info (@GridironInfo_) September 25, 2026 Giants’ young specialists giving Chris Horton something to build on | USAToday.com Dominic Zvada supplied every Giants point in Monday night’s 28-6 loss to the Rams, hitting from 24 yards late in the first half and from 52 in the third quarter. “From the day we got him here, always believed in him, and just needed to get him out there to get him those opportunities,” Horton told reporters on Wednesday. “And we know who he is, he knows who he is. And so, it was very encouraging to get him out there in a game setting and let him kick that 52-yard field goal.” Jordan Stout is the other half of that battery. Horton said the punter’s ability to flip the field has been outstanding, including 70-plus-yard boots and one that approached 80. That only works if the rest of the unit lets it work. “You can’t allow him to do the things that he does if you don’t allow your punt coverage, also those other guys to work,” Horton said. “Situationally, we’re just allowing him to be who he is, and it just starts with everybody understanding what kind of punter we have. We protect the punt, and then we need all-out effort. title: Jamaal Pritchett Gets His Shot
summary: Sometimes all you need is a shot.  They show up every year at NFL camps, hoping for just one shot. One shot to show they belong in a league that has already decided they are unworthy of even a seventh round draft pick. They are the undrafted free agents, and for most of them, playing […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 22: Quinyon Mitchell #27 of the Philadelphia Eagles tackles Jamaal Pritchett #36 of the New York Jets during the second half of a NFL Preseason 2025 game between Philadelphia Eagles and New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on August 22, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The Eagles won 19-17. (Photo by Ishika Samant/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sometimes all you need is a shot. They show up every year at NFL camps, hoping for just one shot. One shot to show they belong in a league that has already decided they are unworthy of even a seventh round draft pick. They are the undrafted free agents, and for most of them, playing in an NFL game is just a dream. The NFL is a tough business to break into. There are only so many roster spots available, and most are taken by draft picks. Most teams realistically have maybe three or four spots up for grab going into training camp, though injuries can open up a few more. Most years a team will bring in ten to fifteen undrafted free agents to compete in training camp, each hoping to defy the odds and secure a spot on an NFL roster. Most are destined to fail, laboring away in obscurity, ending up on practice squads, in other leagues, or out of professional football altogether. For a select few, talent, work ethic and opportunity intersect and an opening presents itself. When it does, the fortunate UDFA must seize the opportunity and immediately impress, or he is likely to have a short run in the NFL. On Sunday an opportunity opens for the Jets’ Jamaal Pritchett. A Jets UDFA originally signed in 2025, Pritchett was signed to the Jets 53 man roster on Saturday after a rash of injuries left the Jets shorthanded at wide receiver. This isn’t the first time Pritchett had to wait patiently for an opportunity. Coming out of high school the 5’ 8”, 175 pound receiver/returner was lightly recruited and had to walk on at South Alabama. He barely saw the field his first year, racking up just two receptions and just 62 all purpose yards. Pritchett was unfazed, working hard at his craft and getting ready for his opportunity, whenever it came. It came quickly. In his second year in 2023 Pritchett got a chance and never looked back. Over the next two years Pritchett had 150 receptions good for 2010 yards. He was tough, shifty and explosive, and he was largely ignored on the national scene. Pritchett was overlooked in the draft process. He was a late add to the Senior Bowl, but impressed after getting his chance. He was then overlooked by all 32 NFL teams in the 2025 NFL draft before the Jets signed him as a UDFA. Given a chance with the Jets, Pritchett again impressed, but was again overlooked. By most accounts he had an excellent training camp in 2025 and did well in the preseason games, only to be cut when the rosters had to be whittled down to 53. Pritchett latched on with the Jets practice squad but never got called up in 2025. He returned to Jets camp in 2026 and again impressed, only to again be cut again in late August. Again Pritchett was signed to the practice squad, but his chances to join the Jets 53 man roster looked bleak after the Jets broke camp with Isaiah Williams, a 2025 Pro Bowler, taking what might have been Pritchett’s spot as a return man. Sometimes all you need is a shot. Pritchett waited and worked. The football gods noticed, and an opportunity arose. The Jets’ wide receiver group had multiple injuries strike over the first two games of the 2026 season. 2026 first round draft pick Omar Cooper Jr went down with an ankle injury in the first game of the season and ended up on injured reserve. 2025 fourth round draft pick Arian Smith followed him to the injured reserve list a game later, as did veteran Tim Patrick. Just like that, the Jets were severely shorthanded at receiver. Pritchett waited for the call. On Saturday, he got it. Jamaal Pritchett had to walk on at South Alabama. He had to fight his way into the Senior Bowl after originally being snubbed. He had to wait through the NFL draft without hearing his name called. He had to sign as an undrafted free agent, play well in his limited opportunities in training camp, then get cut in late August, twice. He had to toil on the Jets practice squad and stay ready, hoping something would open up. On Saturday something opened up. He was signed to the Jets 53 man roster. Pritchett may even get a chance on Sunday to be the Jets’ primary punt returner after Isaiah Williams fumbled two punts last week. Williams had an excellent camp at wide receiver this year, and, with a depleted wide receiver group on Sunday, maybe the Jets give Wiliams a much larger role on offense and relieve him of his punt return duties, at least temporarily. No guarantees, but maybe Pritchett is back fielding punts under the bright lights in Detroit on Sunday. For guys like Pritchett, opportunities are difficult to come by. For many no opening ever arises, and they eventually fade away after laboring in obscurity on NFL practice squads for years, replaced by the next wave of undrafted free agents hoping for just one shot. Pritchett is one of the lucky ones. On Sunday he gets his shot. Let’s see what he can do with it.
author: MacGregor Wells

title: Three things I’m looking at in the Jets vs Lions Game
summary: Who’s ready for some New York Jets football!? I’m not the only one who believes this week is the true test that will help us finally gain an accurate sense of what to expect this season. The young Titans in a new system? Too unproven. The Packers in the rain? Too uncommon. The Detroit Lions, […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - DECEMBER 18: Jamaal Williams #30 of the Detroit Lions runs with the ball as Kwon Alexander #9 of the New York Jets defend during the first half at MetLife Stadium on December 18, 2022 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images Who’s ready for some New York Jets football!? I’m not the only one who believes this week is the true test that will help us finally gain an accurate sense of what to expect this season. The young Titans in a new system? Too unproven. The Packers in the rain? Too uncommon. The Detroit Lions, a dome, and one of the few teams with an unmistakable identity for the past few seasons? Perfect! The best part of this game is that we know what the Lions are. We know how good their players are, how successful their coach has been, and that this team will be playing competitive football in January. To see Aaron Glenn’s Jets beat this team would be indisputable proof that the Jets are on the rise. Even the strongest of Aaron Glenn haters would have to give him his flowers. Now, of course, the Lions have allowed 30+ points in both games played this season, but it’s weird. They were up 21-0 against the Saints before Tyler Shough saved my fantasy team and led the Saints to a much more respectable 31-30 final score. Then they were down 21-0 against the Bills before coming back (not as closely as Shough did) and finishing 41-31. My immediate thought is: how many points can the Jets score against the Lions? How would the Jets respond to being down 14-0, let alone 21-0? With all the offensive weapons on the team, a healthy, cohesive offensive line, and a “gunslinger” at QB, I think we all expected a huge step for the offense this year. 20 points per game is undoubtedly a nice step up from 17.6 last year, but still in the bottom half of the NFL. Aaron Glenn’s Jets have scored 30 points twice (including his head-coaching debut), and it seems they’ll need to cross that threshold to have any chance of beating a team that scored 31 apiece in Weeks 1 and 2. Loose Ends When Frank Reich was hired as the New York Jets’ offensive coordinator, I was excited to see how he’d elevate sophomore tight end Mason Taylor’s production. A couple of months later, the Jets drafted Oregon sensation Kenyon Sadiq with the 16th overall pick and completely lifted the ceiling of this offense. Now he has a 6’5” big body with steady hands, and a 6’3” 240-pound unicorn with 4.39 speed and a developed route tree. Fast forward to this Sunday, and Mason Taylor has been ruled out. Kenyon Sadiq has looked fantastic every time he’s touched the ball, but the problem is he’s touched it only six times in two games. He caught all three of his targets in Week 1 and ran for a TD on his only carry of the game. He had two catches in Week 2, and after one, he hurdled smoothly over a leaping Packers defender. Let’s see how that compares to the other tight ends drafted in the first round recently: Player Overall Pick Year Targets in first 2 games Touches in first 2 games Yards in first 2 games Kyle Pitts 4 2021 14 9 104 Trey McBride 55 2022 0 0 0 Dalton Kincaid 25 2023 10 9 70 Brock Bowers 13 2024 17 15 156 Colston Loveland 10 2025 3 2 12 Tyler Warren 14 2025 16 13 158 Kenyon Sadiq 16 2026 6 6 41 It should be noted that McBride was behind Zach Ertz (14 targets in the first 2 games) on the depth chart, and Colston Loveland was behind Cole Kmet (3 targets in the first 2 games). While Mason Taylor (3 targets in the first two games) has a role, Sadiq is by far the most talented player in the Jets TE room. How glorious would it be to see him get a target count like Kyle Pitts, Brock Bowers, or Tyler Warren? Tyler Warren is especially interesting because he’s the only other player on the chart to have at least one carry in his first two games. Everywhere Frank Reich has gone, tight ends have been a valuable part of the offense, but we have yet to see that develop for the Jets. Perhaps this is the week to get it on track, even without Taylor, since the Lions allowed three catches, 51 yards, and a touchdown to Juwan Johnson to start the year. This past week, those same Lions allowed seven catches, 95 yards, and 1 touchdown to Dalton Kincaid. This is one of those perfect storms where everything should be coming together this week for Kenyon Sadiq to have a much bigger impact on the outcome of this game. Frank Reich’s offense, Mason Taylor’s injury, and Detroit’s leaky defense against opposing tight ends. Will this storm result in raining Sadiq yards and another touchdown? Highly Offensive Jared Goff is currently in the midst of the third-longest active streak of passes without throwing an interception in NFL history. Jahmyr Gibbs is the most popular pick for best running back, while Sam LaPorta and Amon-Ra St. Brown also command respect as elite players in their respective positions. They were the 4th-highest-scoring team per game last year and are in the same spot this year. There’s been a lot of fanfare in the Jets community about having the “league’s top defense,” but I’m here to (regretfully) inform you that stat is misleading. They have allowed the fewest yards, yes, against the league’s second-worst offense full of rookies, and a descending team that was significantly hampered by the rain. I’ve been loving the Jets’ tackling and their overall run defense, but even that may be a mirage when you consider Marshawn Lloyd was starting in his second-ever game and the lowly Titans averaged 4.9 yards per carry. Stopping Detroit will be no easy feat, but the Bills laid out a nice blueprint the Jets could potentially follow. Detroit is built to play with a lead – they have an elite running back and one of the game’s most accurate and composed pocket passers to manage the game. When their run game is flowing, play action opens up the pass game, and they completely dominate the game. Playing from behind is a completely different story for them – they’re forced to throw more, and Goff is forced to take more chances instead of relying on his running backs. This year specifically, the Lions offensive line has declined, so in obvious passing situations they’re less capable of protecting Goff than in previous years. As soon as the Bills scored their opening-drive touchdown, they forced a three-and-out and scored another touchdown. By the time Detroit found any rhythm, the game was already long over, and the Bills kept scoring. The Jets’ best hope is to draw first blood and put the Lions in obvious passing situations so David Bailey and Will McDonald can go to work. Only seven teams in the NFL have more sacks per game than the Jets, and the Jets can climb even higher up the ranks due to Jared Goff’s lack of speed. He’s coming off a game where he was sacked four times, like Jordan Love was when the Jets came in, sacked him three times, and forced a fumble. In this case, offense will certainly be the best form of defense. The more Jared is kept on the sideline, the better. The more they have to throw and abandon the run, the better. If you’re excited about the Jets’ yardage and points-allowed numbers, please let me know in the comments how you think they’ll fare against a team averaging 31 points and 362 yards per game. Chess, Not Checkers My biggest criticism of Aaron Glenn is that he has struggled mightily at the little things that give his team an advantage. Time management, complementary play-calling, and situational decision-making all play a huge role in game outcomes. This isn’t a common skill set – no Jets coach of the last decade succeeded in this area, but it seems like Glenn is especially bad. What makes that interesting is that his former head coach, Dan Campbell, also isn’t that good at it. Dan is super aggressive to a fault and has seen his seasons end because of his reckless, risky decisions. It’s almost as if Aaron Glenn has overcompensated for that as a Head Coach and is now overly cautious and afraid to act when actions need to…
author: thejameswudi

title: Previewing the Jets’ opposition: Detroit Lions
summary: The New York Jets and Detroit Lions are both 1-1 heading into Sunday’s matchup, but both are in search of a bounceback game after the Jets lost in overtime and the Lions gave up 41 points in last Thursday night’s loss to the Bills. Let’s break down the Lions’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 of the Detroit Lions celebrates with Jared Goff #16 after scoring a touchdown against the Buffalo Bills during the third quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets and Detroit Lions are both 1-1 heading into Sunday’s matchup, but both are in search of a bounceback game after the Jets lost in overtime and the Lions gave up 41 points in last Thursday night’s loss to the Bills. Let’s break down the Lions’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks Jared Goff has had three seasons in a row with over 4,500 passing yards and he’s off to a good statistical start so far in 2026. He leads the league with six touchdown passes and doesn’t have an interception. He has been sacked five times and fumbled three times, though. Goff has also been durable. This will be his 72nd consecutive start, dating all the way back to the end of the 2021 season. The Lions moved fast to address their backup situation when Teddy Bridgewater retired in the offseason. His replacement, Josh Dobbs, is an extremely smart quarterback who has started 15 NFL games. Offensive Line The Lions had a trio of starting offensive linemen who were limited in practice this week: Left guard Christian Mahogany, right guard Tate Ratledge and right tackle Blake Miller. However, all three returned to practice on Friday and are expected to start. Mahogany’s return is just in time because Ben Bartch, who started the first two games in his place, is out of this weekend’s game due to injury. He had been struggling in pass protection, so this should be an upgrade, although Mahogany gave up a team-high six sacks in 2025. The first round rookie Miller will make his return after Larry Borom filled in for him last week. He gave up two sacks and had three penalties, so this again looks like it will be an upgrade. Left tackle Penei Sewell is their best lineman, having been to the past four pro bowls. He gave up just two sacks last year. The other starter is Juice Scruggs who is the center, although Cade Mays would probably be starting if he wasn’t on injured reserve. He lines up alongside Ratledge, who led the team in offensive penalties last year. The other backup is guard Miles Frazier, who was a fifth round pick last year. They will also need to elevate another one with Bartch ruled out. Running Backs The two-headed monster is no more, as David Montgomery is now in Houston, but this has freed up Jahmyr Gibbs to try and establish himself as the league’s best running back. He’s off to a decent start with 299 yards from scrimmage in the first two games. With new addition Isiah Pacheco on injured reserve, the number two is the converted safety Sione Vaki, although he has only 10 carries in three seasons. Jacob Saylors is the number three, but mostly on the team for his special teams abilities. Pass catchers Pro bowler Amon-Ra St. Brown is off to an excellent start this year. He leads the NFL with 19 catches and four touchdown receptions. He’s by no means the Lions’ only weapon, though, as Jameson Williams is also coming off back-to-back thousand-yard seasons. Then you have tight end Sam LaPorta, who had 17 touchdowns in his first two seasons before missing eight games last year. Detroit’s other starting receiver, Isaac TeSlaa, only caught 16 passes last year but six of them were touchdowns and he’s established himself as a big play threat and capable of highlight reel grabs. Tay Martin and Tom Kennedy are also both on the team at wide receiver but neither has played an offensive snap so far this season. Depth at tight end comes from ex-Jet Tyler Conklin, Jackson Meeks and Brock Wright. Wright, who also plays fullback, caught a crucial touchdown pass when the 2022 Jets blew a late lead to the Lions in the last meeting between these teams. Defensive Line Former number two overall pick Aidan Hutchinson is the star of the Lions defensive line. He had 14.5 sacks last year and already has three in the first two games of this season. DJ Wonnum is the other starting edge with second round pick Derrick Moore on the bench along with another rookie, the undrafted Eric O’Neill. Ahmed Hassanein was inactive last Thursday. Tyler Lacy is also listed as an edge but he’s 300 pounds and also plays inside. In addition, the Lions also have former first round pick Payton Turner, but he’s on injured reserve. The starters on the interior are Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams. McNeill’s importance is evident by the fact that he’s easily Detroit’s highest paid defensive player. Sixth round rookie Skyler Gill-Howard provides depth off the bench along with Levi Onwuzurike. Mekhi Wingo is also on the roster but was inactive against the Bills. Linebackers The linebacker unit is anchored by all-pro Jack Campbell, who had 176 tackles last season. Derrick Barnes is the other starter and he’s had an effective start to the season with 13 tackles, two pass breakups, two sacks and an interception in the first two games. Depth comes from Trevor Nowaske, Malcolm Rodriguez and the experienced Devin White. Fourth round pick Jimmy Rolder has been inactive so far, though. Defensive Backs The Lions have serious issues in their secondary, which is the main reason they have given up the second highest yardage total and points total in the first two games. Safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, each of whom were pro bowlers in 2024, began the year on the PUP list, so the Jets have known for some time Detroit would be undermanned in the secondary for this game. However, Avonte Maddox, who was filling in, suffered a season-ending foot injury in the Bills game and, as if that wasn’t bad enough, his replacement Thomas Harper is also out of Sunday’s game due to an ankle issue. Options that remain include ex-Jets Chuck Clark and Jalen Mills. Clark started the first two games but Mills was only just added to the practice squad a few days ago. Offseason addition Christian Izien may need to step up, while undrafted rookie Bishop Fitzgerald is also an option. The Lions are theoretically at full strength in terms of the cornerback position but their starting trio – DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin and slot corner Roger McCreary all lack size which could be an issue against some of the multiple tight end looks the Jets run. Fifth round rookie Keith Abney II, Khalil Dorsey and Ennis Rakestraw Jr. provide depth at corner. Special Teams Kicker Jake Bates has made all 10 of his kicks so far this season, but he missed nine in 2025. He has a big leg but was just 4-for-9 from beyond 50 last season. Punter Jack Fox, a pro bowler in 2020 and 2024, is off to a solid start after his numbers dropped off a bit in 2025. Longtime return specialist (and former Jet) Kalif Raymond is now with the Bears, so the Lions have Kennedy and Saylors returning kicks. Kennedy has handled punts so far, with the kickoff duties shared. Nobody has broken a long one yet this year. Martin and Dorsey are the team’s primary punt gunners and Martin leads the team with four special teams tackles so far this season. Nowaske, Vaki and Saylors were productive in kick coverage last year.

title: Eagles Film Preview: Offense should have good opportunities against this Bears defense
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 28: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles rolls out to throw a pass during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Lincoln Financial Field on November 28, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images | Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. The Bears’ defense has a clear personality. Dennis Allen wants to pressure the quarterback, play aggressively behind it, and trust his corners to survive tough outside matchups. I can see plenty of opportunities to score. The Bears have some good individual defenders, but I don’t think they have the talent across the back end to play this aggressively without giving up chances in both the passing and running game. Pass Defense The first thing that stands out is how willing the Bears are to leave their outside corners exposed. They have played man coverage on 43.3% of snaps through two games, more than double the league average, and they have frequently shown a single-high safety behind it. This isn’t a defense that spends the whole game protecting its corners with two safeties deep. Allen wants to challenge receivers, crowd the line of scrimmage, and make the quarterback beat tight coverage before the rush arrives. Jaylon Johnson has allowed the most receiving yards of any corner through two weeks, and while I would never judge a player entirely by that number, I can see the problems on film. Some of it is Johnson’s play; some of it is the position the scheme puts him in. If the Bears keep leaving him isolated outside, the Eagles have to test him. This should be a week for Jalen Hurts to give his receivers opportunities down the sideline. Bears' Defense All22 Thread. 1) They are very vulnerable on the outside. Jaylon Johnson has given up the most yards in the NFL through 2 weeks. It's a combination of scheme and individual play, but the Eagles should absolutely take some shots outside this week. pic.twitter.com/DgHvX6f0EB — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 26, 2026 Tyrique Stevenson has had problems outside, too. The Panthers attacked the Bears with variations of double moves and were very successful. When a corner is playing aggressively with limited help behind him, one false step can become a huge play. I would like to see the Eagles use bunches and switch releases to give Dontayvion Wicks and DeVonta Smith cleaner releases, then take shots once they have established those threats. Stevenson hurt his hamstring against the Vikings and was limited in Friday’s practice, so I would avoid assuming either that he will play or that he is out. If he does play, the Eagles should still test how well he can turn and run. Smith was also limited on Friday with a hamstring injury, so that matchup will depend on both players’ health by Monday. 3) I mentioned Jalyon Johnson, but Tyrique Stevenson has also struggled on the outside. Some of this is scheme-related, though, as I said above. They play a lot of single-high man coverage and leave their outside corners on an island. The Panthers took advantage with a lot of… pic.twitter.com/luShG6VQor — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 26, 2026 I wasn’t especially impressed when the Bears moved away from man coverage, either. There have been communication errors in zone, and it is still early enough in the season for offenses to stress their coverage rules with motion and formation changes. The Eagles should find out how the Bears handle receivers crossing the formation and how quickly their defenders pass routes off to one another. If Allen responds by playing man, the Eagles get the individual matchups they should want. If he plays zone, there are chances to test the communication. 2) They play a lot of man coverage, and I wasn't overly impressed watching them in zone when they did go to it. I think you can test their communication, since it is still early in the season and they have had some busts similar to the Titans'. pic.twitter.com/pASA7OxJtx — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 26, 2026 One young defensive back I would be careful about challenging unnecessarily is Malik Muhammad. Rookie slot corner Muhammad has probably been the Bears’ best player in the secondary through two games. His interception against the Panthers was unbelievable, and he has already shown he can contribute as a blitzer. He was a fourth-round pick, but he does not look like a player the Eagles should target simply because he is inexperienced. My preference is to work the outside matchups and make Allen decide how much help he is prepared to give his corners. 4) However, you have to be very careful targeting slot corner Malik Muhammad, who has probably been their best player in the secondary this season. This is an outstanding interception against the Panthers. He's played well through two weeks. Pretty remarkable for a 4th-round… pic.twitter.com/TKgCvva5aJ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 26, 2026 Dayo Odeyingbo was their most effective starting edge rusher against the Vikings, while Grady Jarrett remains capable of causing problems inside. Montez Sweat is still a player the Eagles must account for, and Austin Booker made an impact in limited opportunities last week. However, this does not look like a front that consistently overwhelms offensive lines with four rushers. They aren’t that talented. That does not mean the Eagles can ignore Allen’s pressure packages. His double A-gap mug looks, with linebackers lined up over both sides of the center, are designed to make the protection declare itself before the offense knows who is actually rushing. A defender who appears ready to blitz can drop out, while pressure comes from somewhere else. Even without an elite four-man rush, this defense can win if the quarterback hesitates and the receivers take too long to separate. I would expect Hurts and the Eagles’ offensive line to spend plenty of time identifying those looks before the snap. 5) As I said, they don't have an elite pass rush, but this type of defense can get a lot of clean-up sacks if your receivers don't win. It's an aggressive defensive style. Dennis Allen uses double A-gap mug fronts as a staple in obvious passing situations. It can be hard to tell… pic.twitter.com/tA2f1FMEcH — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 26, 2026 Hurts needs to know where his quick throw is if the Bears bring more rushers than the Eagles can block. The receivers need routes that can win quickly against man coverage. I also want the Eagles to remain willing to use play-action and attack vertically when they have earned the opportunity. The Bears were happy to play aggressive single-high coverage against the Vikings, even with Justin Jefferson outside. That gives an offense chances if its receivers win early or the linebackers take a step toward the run. The Bears have allowed explosive passes on 11.9% of pass plays through two weeks. They are giving opponents chances. 6) Again, look at the aggressive single-high man coverage. You'll have chances to create big plays as an offense if the play-action works or your receivers win early. This is an aggressive coverage call for a defense facing a team with Justin Jefferson on the outside! pic.twitter.com/GBhQtkM7O0 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 26, 2026 Run Defense The Bears’ run defense is inconsistent. They have allowed negative EPA per rush, suggesting they have prevented the really damaging outcomes overall, but opponents still succeeded on 58.7% of their runs. Aaron Jones gained 105 yards on 23 carries last week. I noticed problems setting the edge in both games, particularly on…
