title: Five Washington players crucial to Commanders upsetting Seahawks
summary: The Commanders are missing a bunch of key pieces for Sunday’s home opener against the Seattle Seahawks. They ruled five players out. All of them are every-down players or significant contributors. All of them you’d consider starters.   That creates a situation where Washington needs replacements to capitalize on extra playing time or healthy top […]
full_text: The Commanders are missing a bunch of key pieces for Sunday’s home opener against the Seattle Seahawks. They ruled five players out . All of them are every-down players or significant contributors. All of them you’d consider starters. That creates a situation where Washington needs replacements to capitalize on extra playing time or healthy top players to dominate in order to compete with the reigning Super Bowl champs. This isn’t an easy opponent and Seattle’s arrival in Washington is ill-timed considering Washington’s injury situation. The Commanders must find a way to emerge victorious, which would be easier with significant contributions from these five guys (not named Marcus Mariota). Let’s take a look at five Commanders key to victory on Sunday at Northwest Stadium: EDGE K’Lavon Chaisson It’s safe to say at this point that Commanders pressure is the best coverage. Washington’s pass-rushers must get home on a regular-basis to make the Seahawks offense uncomfortable, especially with quarterback Sam Darnold back and Jaxon Smith-Njigba as the NFL’s most dangerous receiver. Chaisson has an excellent 18.6% pressure rate that leads all Washington pass rushers. He’s getting to the quarterback and being a disruptive force. A few plays from him (sacks, forced fumbles and errant throws) can change the course of Sunday’s game in the Commanders’ favor. They’ll need those in a big way after failing to generate a turnover on Sunday. Chaisson’s just the man to get them. RB Rachaad White Veteran running back and relatively new addition Rachaad White was the best Commanders running back in Week 2, proving the most efficient and explosive running back and receiver out of the backfield. It’s time to roll with White, especially early, and see if he can’t get some momentum going with a high touch volume of carries and quick receptions. I’m not suggesting Washington bench Bill Croskey-Merritt. He’s still part of the game plan, but let’s see if sticking with a primary back can get the run game going and provide an option out of the backfield to keep that position productive against a super-tough Seahawks front. DB Quan Martin It sure seems like Quan Martin will see significant snaps with Jeremy Reaves on Sunday due to Nick Cross’s injury. We might see Percy Butler in there some, but it sure seems like a safe bet Martin’s gonna be a feature player. And, yeah, we know that scares the fan base to death. Even if there’s pessimism surrounding this deep tandem, Martin must prove the doubters wrong and be a productive and functional member of this secondary. A takeaway wouldn’t hurt. And definitely no blown coverages. Yeah, that isn’t a high bar, but Martin must be an asset, especially with such an instrumental player like Cross out. DL Daron Payne Go read Mark Tyler’s Studs and Duds for an honest performance review of Daron Payne from Week 2. He said that Payne gave zero effort against Dallas. He had a 4.8% pressure rate versus 21.1% the week before, per NFL Pro. It could’ve been a disadvantageous matchup against Dallas, but the difference also shows how good Payne can be when he’s at his best, even at this stage of his career. Washington needs the dominant version against the run and pass to help win battles up front and keep Seattle’s point totals down. WR Terry McLaurin Terry McLaurin was on this list last week. Repeats are typically avoided, but it’s worth repeating here because of a second straight inefficient game. He had two catches for 50 yards on nine targets against Dallas. While not every situation was to be blamed on him, the Commanders and McLaurin must find ways to use the receiver’s ability on crucial downs, while finding him with space to run after the catch. He’s the team’s most dynamic skill player, and must be better than the first two outings. He can dominate a game. Doing so in Week 3 would be key.

full_text: The Washington Commanders announced they are elevating one player for Sunday’s home opener against the Seattle Seahawks. The team designated Ale Kaho as a standard practice-squad elevation on Saturday. That makes sense considering their lack of depth at linebacker, with Frankie Luvu out with a groin injury and Jordan Magee on injured reserve. Sonny Styles and Leo Chenal should play nearly every snap on the interior, with Kain Medrano and Kaho in reserve. That also helps bolster the special teams. This is Kaho’s second elevation, with a maximum of three possible in one season. He’ll revert back to the practice squad after the Week 3 game, and can still be elevated one more time without having to sign him to the 53-man roster. The Commanders released their injury report Friday and ruled out five players: QB Jayden Daniels (elbow), RG Sam Cosmi (concussion), S Nick Cross (illness), TE Chig Okonkwo (hamstring), and LB Frankie Luvu (groin). (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 26 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Jayden Daniels braces for the short term; what’s next long term? The Athletic (paywall) By the end of Week 3, I project we will have seen 38 starting quarterbacks this season. That is one more than we saw three weeks into last year. It’s also mostly in line with each of the last five seasons. So why does this feel different? Chicago, New York and Washington, to start. “It was three massive markets with interesting young players,” one league source says. “And it was all bad timing. All those games were relatively popular. You have three highly famous markets, with big players, with high-visibility (television) windows. It will feel worse than it is.” The brace Daniels will eventually wear will restrict his arm (and elbow) from fully extending, but it should not limit what he has to do on the field. Daniels wore a brace on his left arm upon his return from the same injury last season; he will have to wear a bulkier one this go-round. He is being labeled as week to week, but the team departs for its Week 4 game against the Indianapolis Colts in London on Tuesday evening. If he isn’t on the plane, he will be ruled out. If he makes the trip, that means, at the very least, he is beginning to practice with the brace. It is possible, depending on how the rest of the year unfolds, that Daniels has surgery after the season and is fully prepared for the 2027 season. The injury…muddies the waters on a potential contract extension. [A] league source: “I would wait to pay him until I see him fully healthy. I’m OK overspending on the QB position if I’m sure on the guy, because the difference in $70 million per year versus $75 million is nonexistent. If they have to wait, so be it. title: Outlining a plan to address the Washington Commanders secondary
summary: Things have not gone according to plan for the Washington Commanders and their secondary through the first two weeks of the season. The idea of frequent and disguised pressures shouldering the bulk of the burden for the defensive backs is not sustainable if teams can slow the pressure and exploit coverage lapses, and there have […]
full_text: Things have not gone according to plan for the Washington Commanders and their secondary through the first two weeks of the season. The idea of frequent and disguised pressures shouldering the bulk of the burden for the defensive backs is not sustainable if teams can slow the pressure and exploit coverage lapses, and there have been plenty to exploit. As many fans will tell you, the ship has sailed on any significant personnel additions at this point in the season, but in this article I will outline how defensive coordinator Daronte Jones could try to fix the issues in the secondary with the players he currently has on the roster. The most difficult part of the plan is it requires the coaching staff to make personnel changes instead of dispensing platitudes and focusing on communication and leveling up . It also needs to happen quickly, before the team is 0-4 to start the season. Listening to Daronte Jones’ last press conference , I don’t know if they feel the same urgency to make the necessary changes. Daronte Jones on when it's time to think lineup changes: "You've got to first dive into why is it happening, and then if it's become 'Hey, this guy's just not doing what we're asking him to do, then you may have to make a personnel change in that regards" pic.twitter.com/GoGcp2n4xv — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) September 24, 2026 Still, here is what I think Jones should do if he decides to switch things up, using Hogs Haven writer MattInBrisVegas’s wonderful Stats and Snaps series as our guide. Bench Mike Sainristil After the first two games, Mike Sainristil currently has a 153.7 allowed passer rating, is ranked 94th out of 94 CBs by PFF , and is coming off a atrocious performance last week where Pro Football Reference assigned him 3.07 Y/Cov Snp . Hogs Haven’s Mark Tyler has some interesting ideas on what to do with Mikey, but with the goal of improving the secondary immediately, I am going with the bench option. It might be wise for Jones to assign Sainristil nothing but slot reps in practice and see if he can work his way back into the lineup, but for now he needs to sit. Out Nick Cross Initially, I had a different version of this plan put together, one that included Cross as a key piece of the puzzle, but with the news he was hospitalized after the Cowboys game and ruled out completely on Wednesday, I think Commanders fans should not plan on him being part of the solution for a couple of weeks. So what’s the plan? If we look at Matt’s tables from this week’s article, we can identify what positions Jones will need to fill this week versus Seattle after removing two starters. Mike Sainristil played the majority of his snaps at LCB, but there are also some slot and box snaps that need to be accounted for as well. Nick Cross moved around the secondary but was the team’s primary slot defender. So we need to look at three different roles: LCB , Slot/Box , and FS . LCB Jones has already been trending towards the first move by giving Rasul Douglas more snaps last week. The veteran cornerback hasn’t been perfect, but PFR has him with a more palatable 97.4 allowed passer rating. Matt’s data from the Cowboys game tells us that Douglas had a bad day in coverage, allowing 5 targets and 4 receptions for 52 yds in 18 coverage snaps (2.89 Y/Cov Snp), but I would think a good chunk of the allowed yards came from this play where he read the route wrong. CeeDee Lamb and the Cowboys had Rasul Douglas (29) fooled on this one. Turpin's clear route makes it look like it's designed to free Lamb on the in-breaking route. 88 sells it beautifully. Great tendency breaker. pic.twitter.com/F0UzsYGDSm — Mauricio Rodríguez (@MauNFL) September 21, 2026 While this certainly is not what you want to see, the remainder of his reps were better and Douglas would be a step up for what we have seen from Sainristil on the boundary. The thought would be to have Rasul work almost completely on the outside, as he has done for most of his career and find another option at the slot position. Slot/Box Last season, when corner Jeff Odukah went out with a concussion, the Vikings elevated Fabian Moreau from the practice squad to the active roster. The 32-year-old veteran did surprisingly well playing limited snaps there, posting very respectable containment numbers (0.51 Y/Cov Snap) and a 54.6 allowed passer rating on 152 coverage snaps. Across 152 coverage snaps, Moreau allowed 8 receptions on 16 targets for a total of 53 yards, a long reception of 11 yards, no TDs, and only committed 1 penalty per PFF — BREVY BRIGHTLIGHTS (@brevmanbane) May 20, 2026 Moreau was brought in as a break glass in case of emergency option as the veteran who knows Jones’ system after two seasons with the Vikings. Unfortunately, I think we have reached that point. Limiting Fabian’s snaps would be important, but the 6’0”, 204-pound Moreau could provide some solid ones as a big nickel. Jeremy Reaves was initially one of my players to bench, as his 158.7 allowed pass rating is one of the worst in the league, but with Nick Cross sidelined, there is a void in the total snap count for the secondary. The fix is to play Reaves in the box with little to no snaps at the free safety position. Jeremy is still a very physical player and can trigger downhill in run support and the short-to-intermediate parts of the field. I don’t love this solution, but it could work until Cross returns from injury. Free Safety Here is where the plan gets a little thin. The team never accounted for the free safety role in their roster planning during the offseason with Martin or Harris potentially filling the role but ultimately ended up demoting Martin, releasing Harris, and going with Jeremy Reaves in their place. With Reaves relegated to the box, the team needs to find another player at free safety. Tyler Owens has been a career special teamer so far, but still might be the best option to replace Reaves and Cross in the deep part of the field. He has the size, speed, and athleticism, but in his one chance last season he looked lost in his assignments. #Commanders S Tyler Owens Most snaps in career (25) Most coverage snaps in career (15) 3 sacks 1 STOP 2 targets 2 receptions long 18yds #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/HTGx7IrYle — Deuce_Redzone (@redzoneinthelab) October 29, 2025 The thing to note here is that Owens played heavily up by the line of scrimmage and in the slot, instead of in a free safety role. In fact, according to Matt’s write-up for last season’s matchup versus the Chiefs he played none at the position. In a role that keeps the play in front of him, limits his reads, and allows him to utilize his range, Owens could potentially perform significantly better. Quan Martin hasn’t been quite as bad as Sainristil through two games, with a 118.7 allowed passer rating per Pro Football Reference . The catch is he has played about half the total number of snaps as Mikey. PFF has him ranked 83rd out of 84 safeties. He was also initially on my bench list as well but also gets a pass with Cross out as the team will likely need him here for two high safety looks, if they decide not to play Reaves there. Coaching & Communication The Washington Commanders decided to retain defensive backs/safeties coach Tom Donatell during the offseason while promoting William Gay from assistant coach to defensive backs/cornerbacks coach. The two decisions were surprising given the secondary’s performance last year and Donatell’s previous track record with the San Diego Chargers. Daronte Jones’ previous ties to defensive coordinator Ed Donatell may have added a layer of familiarity after LSU safeties coach Jake Olsen changed his mind about accepting an offer to join Washington’s coaching staff. Whatever the reason, the two coaches do not seem to be successful installing coverage and communication techniques and Jones will have to take valuable time away from developing his defensive game plan to correct it. Communication issues have been a persistent problem for…

title: Commanders fans split on Jayden Daniels return – poll results
summary: Most weeks of the year, and every week of the season for several years now, Hogs Haven runs Reacts surveys, and I write an article breaking down the results. Because I’m writing about what Hogs Haven readers have said in a collective sense, I rely heavily on the comments section to inform what I write. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 20: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders warms up before a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Most weeks of the year, and every week of the season for several years now, Hogs Haven runs Reacts surveys, and I write an article breaking down the results . Because I’m writing about what Hogs Haven readers have said in a collective sense, I rely heavily on the comments section to inform what I write . The collective opinion expressed in the survey may not always match my own, but I try to offer an honest peek into the reasons behind the numbers as best I can make sense of them . This week, I want to take a slightly different approach to analyzing the survey results, as you’ll see in the article below. This week, we asked two questions , which is our norm during the regular season. Question 1: Fan confidence The first question asked, as it does every week of the season (at least until early December), whether you are confident in the team’s direction . From our first survey to our second—before and after the opener in Philadelphia—confidence actually climbed from 70% to 83%. That early surge seemed based entirely on the “quality” of the loss: Washington went on the road against an elite Eagles team, pushed them to the brink in a 24-22 nail-biter, and looked competitive throughout. The general feeling was that the outcome turned on a handful of fixable execution errors. This week, however, confidence collapsed to just 20%. A 37-20 loss in Dallas will do that to a fan base. The defense looked disjointed, the secondary surrendered big plays through the air, and the interior offensive line struggled in short-yardage spots. To make matters worse, franchise quarterback Jayden Daniels suffered another dislocation to his left elbow on the final play of the first half. Ron's teams went 7-9, 7-10, & 8-8-1 in his first three years here. His QBs were Smith, Haskins (RIP), Heinicke, Wentz, & Kyle Allen. He didn't have Jayden Daniels and his teams those first years never went through a 2-12 stretch. You take 5 from AP/DQ, they've been outdone by RR. — Oz (@OBtoojiveforyou) September 23, 2026 Sitting at 0-2 overall and 0-2 in the NFC East with the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks arriving in Landover for the home opener, fans are not, to put it mildly, feeling optimistic. Question 2: Jayden Daniels’ 2026 outlook The second question in our survey asked whether you believe Jayden Daniels’ 2026 season came to an end with his injury in Dallas. Visit our partners at FanDuel In a roughly 60:40 split, the majority of survey respondents — who voted in the poll before any update or decision was announced by the team — believed that Jayden would return to the field at some point this season. Again, voting took place early in the week before we had much official word from the team. On Friday, GM Adam Peters gave an update on his weekly radio appearance, and later in the day, head coach Dan Quinn provided confirmation on Daniels’ status. It turns out that the 59% of fans who expected Jayden to return this season were right, at least, according to both AP and DQ, though the exact timing of his return remains up in the air aside from the fact that he is not being placed on IR at the moment. The significance of not being put on injured reserve As you are probably aware, players who are on IR must miss at least 4 games. For Daniels, a stint on IR would have meant Weeks 3 to 6, followed by a bye in Week 7, with a return allowed no earlier than Week 8 at home against the Eagles. The fact that he is not being put on IR signals that the team expects him to return to play earlier, meaning in Week 4, 5 or 6, against the Colts in London, Giants in Landover, or the 49ers in San Francisco. Yes, London remains on the table. Just have to wait/see. https://t.co/yWNXYRay4V — John Keim (@john_keim) September 25, 2026 The Noah Brown lesson Of course, we all remember WR Noah Brown, who, last season, was injured in the Week 2 game vs the Packers. He was not immediately placed on IR, indicating that the team expected him to return by the Week 6 game in mid-October. Instead, when that mid-October date arrived, Brown was not activated, instead being put on IR on October 15th and staying there until early December. So, while it is clear that Adam Peters, Dan Quinn and Jayden himself all expect or hope for his return to play sometime in October, the example of Noah Brown from last season reminds us that return from injury is an uncertain process. In any event, one thing is clear — the team, like the majority of our survey respondents — expect Jayden to be back as captain and quarterback in the coming weeks. Commanders fans: Make your pick in the SB Nation app! Take Reacts surveys, create Commanders polls, and see how your answers compare with fellow Hogs Haven fans. Then discuss the results with the Burgundy and Gold community. Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . An experiment: Mapping 740+ comments with AI As I noted at the top, I try to integrate the thoughts of survey respondents into these weekly articles. This week, I faced both a challenge and an interesting opportunity. The survey article generated over 210 comments on Tuesday and Wednesday. Meanwhile, Monday’s All aTwitter post had drawn more than 530 comments following the Dallas game and covering much of the same territory. Across just 72 hours, this community posted roughly three-quarters of a million words dissecting the state of the franchise in the context of Daniels’ (re)injury. Rather than cherry-picking 4 or 5 comments and calling it a day, I decided to try something different. Having read so much about how Artificial Intelligence is revolutionizing work flows around the world, I figured I could ‘opt in’ and make the revolution work for me. I fed all 530+ comments from Monday’s All aTwitter and all 210+ comments from the Reacts thread into Gemini, asking it to summarize the arguments and track how community sentiment evolved as the week progressed. I know there is plenty of justifiable skepticism across the internet about AI content replacing human writers. Rest assured, I am not handing over my keyboard, but as an analytical tool for mapping community psychology, it seemed like the perfect opportunity to integrate some of the latest technology into my decidedly low-tech writing. What follows in the italicized block below is the AI-generated synthesis of your comments across both threads: The community breakdown (generated via Comment Text Analysis) 1. Immediate aftermath: The Monday vent (All aTwitter) Following the Dallas game, comments reflected acute shock, in-game tactical frustration, and heated debate over Daniels: The Daniels status debate: Discussion split between a minority urging Daniels to get fitted with a brace and return immediately to protect his developmental momentum (LionRoars1987 citing Kurt Warner) and a strong majority rejecting that path, citing re-injury risk and pain. Debate also sparked over whether awkwardly planting an arm is a recurring durability issue or an unavoidable fluke. In-game frustrations: Sharp criticism focused on end-of-half clock management—specifically Daniels trying to make a play rather than taking an easy field goal—leaving the team down 7 rather than 4. Commenters tallied missed opportunities and called out interior offensive line failures in short-yardage spots under center. Commenters vented about Dan Quinn’s game management, with a few floating early speculation about offensive coordinator David Blough. 2. title: NFL Week 3 betting guide: Analysis and top plays for Sunday's games
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 3 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game-winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 3.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week  | Solak's plays  | Walder's props 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 Kansas City Chiefs at Miami Dolphins (-10.5, 46.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Hard Rock Stadium, Miami Gardens, Fla.

 

 I tend to stay away from double-digit spreads in this league (especially for road favorites). That can be bad business given the talent level and coaching we get on Sundays. But looking at the matchup and scheme advantages with Kansas City, I'm in on Andy Reid's team. I'll give you my quick notes for both clubs, along with some player props.

 

 When the Chiefs have the ball: The offseason addition of Kenneth Walker III has given the Chiefs a true difference-maker with dual-threat traits in the backfield. Walker has rushed for at least 117 yards -- with at least 23 carries -- in both games this season, and in a Week 2 win over the Indianapolis Colts he caught six of 10 targets for 61 yards. We can expect Walker to get his touches on the ground against a Miami defense giving up 112.5 rushing yards per game (18th in the NFL), which allows Reid's unit to control offensive tempo.

 In the pass game, I see clear matchup advantages for the Chiefs. The Dolphins are giving up an average of 8.6 YPA (30th in the NFL), and they play man coverage at a rate of 58.9% (fourth most). Look for Reid to set up his receivers for catch-and-run throws from Patrick Mahomes , with Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce working multiple levels of the field against a Miami secondary that lacks high-end talent.

 When Miami has the ball: The Dolphins have struggled to build offensive rhythm and lack an identity, having failed to score more than 13 points in each of their first two games. Running back De'Von Achane has rushed for a total of 110 yards this season, and we aren't seeing his elite pass-catching ability (he has only 49 yards receiving). Quarterback Malik Willis has shown flashes, but his accuracy has been inconsistent (completing 58% of his passes), and he has thrown only one touchdown pass.

 Now, Miami does have some young talent in the pass game with Malik Washington , Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell , but Douglas has been ruled out for this matchup after missing practice all week with an ankle injury. The Dolphins lack a proven No. 1 who can win critical game situations at a high rate and they average only 183.5 passing yards per game. Now they'll face a multiple Chiefs defense -- one that leans on late movement and schemed pressure. This Kansas City defense is giving up 90 yards rushing per game and only 5.5 YPA. Miami will need to find a way to create positive game flow while producing some explosive plays to stay in this one.

 

 Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

 Rashee Rice receiving yards OVER 47.5 (-114) 

 Rice, who caught four of six targets for 83 yards in the Week 2 win over the Colts, could have early opportunities against the Dolphins' single-high man coverages. Rice can turn an underneath throw into an explosive gain.

 Travis Kelce receptions OVER 4.5 receptions (-114) 

 Kelce's play speed looked different last week against the Colts, both in the route stem and after the catch. Kelce caught nine of 11 targets in that game, using his high-end coverage awareness to find open grass. He should be a priority target again for Mahomes on Sunday.

 Tyquan Thornton anytime TD (+475) 

 I'm thinking of a shot-play throw here to Thornton on Sunday. Thornton caught all four of his targets for 86 yards last week against the Colts, so look for Reid to set up him on a deep-ball concept in Miami.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Baltimore Ravens -3.5 (-105) vs. Dallas Cowboys 

 Injuries are important to watch heading into this game. Not one of WR Zay Flowers , OT Ronnie Stanley or OLB Trey Hendrickson practiced Wednesday for the Ravens. Still, head coach Jesse Minter said after practice that he feels "like we will have a good shot with a lot of guys this week."

 

 Assuming the Ravens are relatively close to full strength, I like their matchup against Dallas quite a bit. The Cowboys' back seven has struggled tremendously through two weeks of the Christian Parker era on defense; it's a challenging defensive scheme, and they are generally lacking for team speed. Their light edge rushers can be targeted in the run game. Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has excelled at two things so far: attacking the edge in the running game, and generating YAC opportunities for Flowers. Baltimore might steamroll the Cowboys.

 I'm a little worried about the travel and field in Brazil, which can introduce some chaos. The Cowboys' offense can also score in bunches. But the Ravens are a better pressure team, thanks to the play of Hendrickson and Minter's willingness to send pressures on key downs. I like them to get enough stops in what should be a high-scoring affair.

 I'd take this up to -4 (-110), but only if we get positive injury news throughout the week.

 Houston Texans -1.5 (-118) at Indianapolis Colts 

 Two 0-2 division rivals seemingly with their seasons already on the line -- intense stuff for Week 3. I admired the Colts' pluck in their game against the Chiefs, but the Texans' defense is made of far stiffer stuff. Houston has won the last five games between the teams, though QB  Daniel Jones was hurt for the most recent matchup.

 

 The Colts have relied heavily on big-play receiver Alec Pierce to generate explosive plays against DeMeco Ryans' aggressive defense. Last season against the Texans across two games, Pierce had eight catches, 210 yards and three touchdowns. Pierce hurt his heel against the Chiefs and is on injured reserve, which puts all the more pressure on Josh Downs , Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell at receiver. It's hard to imagine the Colts finding the same big plays that the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals have against this Texans secondary.

 It looks like star receiver Nico Collins will miss another week with a hamstring injury, which has pulled this line down to -1.5 after opening at -2.5 and flirting with -3 throughout the week. I'm still on the Texans' side here -- their offense moved the ball much better against Cincinnati defense than the scoreboard would indicate (35.1% success rate was far better than the Bengals' 27.6% on the day). The Colts' linebacker room is such a liability that I expect C.J. Stroud to still have a strong day working the middle of the field.

 David Montgomery anytime TD (-110), 2+ TD scorer (+550) 

 I'm thrilled to get Montgomery back down near even money after the Texans' absolute stinker against the Bengals in Week 2. Montgomery's number is low this week out of fear of another inept offensive day without Collins, but the Texans weren't all that bad on offense. One drive ended at the Bengals' 16-yard line on a fumbled field goal try. Another ended on the Bengals' 18 on a fourth-and-1 run failure. Another resulted in a field goal from the Bengals' 19, a fearful attempt on fourth-and-1 as the Bengals were dominating in short yardage. So, the Texans moved the ball a lot more effectively than…

title: NFL Week 3 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines
summary: Touchdowns for Kenneth Walker III and Xavier Worthy? The Broncos pulling an upset of the Rams? Fantasy value for C.J. Stroud? And a big day from Geno Smith?
full_text:
Week 3 of the  2026 NFL season is underway after the Falcons beat the Packers on Thursday night . But what will happen in the remaining 15 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks two underdogs who could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projects stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody gives three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen predicts three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out four wild-card predictions.

 Could the Broncos upset the Rams? Will the Chiefs' Kenneth Walker III and Xavier Worthy score against the Dolphins? Is Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud a fantasy sleeper against the Colts? And could the most entertaining game of the week be ... Raiders-Saints? Let's make 15 big predictions for all of Sunday and Monday's action.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Other predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts two upsets 
 

 Denver Broncos +2.5 (+114) vs. Los Angeles Rams 

 Denver has the defensive formula to win this. With wide receiver  Puka Nacua likely sidelined ( groin ), Broncos cornerback  Pat Surtain II  can focus on Davante Adams . Meanwhile, Denver's pass rush can attack a vulnerable Rams offensive line. That pressure could keep Matthew Stafford from finding the rhythm he showed against the Giants .

 On the other side of the ball, Broncos quarterback  Bo Nix can use quick throws to find wide receiver  Jaylen Waddle and avoid long third downs.

 
 

 

 Dallas Cowboys +3.5 (+135) vs. Baltimore Ravens 

 The Cowboys' path is to make Baltimore play from behind in Rio de Janeiro. That shouldn't be hard since the sharpness of QB  Dak Prescott and Dallas' passing game gives the team a real chance to score early, putting more pressure on Lamar Jackson and a Ravens offensive line that struggled against New Orleans. The Cowboys' biggest concern is holding up against the Ravens' rushing attack.

 

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 Abdul Carter , Edge, New York Giants : 2.0 sacks, 6 pressures, 27% pass rush win rate

 Carter's rookie season was noteworthy because, despite just 4.0 sacks, he finished top-10 in pass rush win rate at edge. That was a strong sign about the player he could become, and that signal has persisted in Year 2.

 Carter ranks 11th in pass rush win rate at edge and is tied for the fifth-most pass rush wins among all players. In Week 3 , Carter gets the chance to run after second-year quarterback  Cam Ward , whose 8.8% sack rate since the start of last season ranks third worst among qualifying quarterbacks.

 
 

 Xavier Worthy , WR, Kansas City Chiefs : 5 targets, 3 receptions, 64 yards, 1 touchdown

 Worthy's production has been lackluster to start the season, but that could easily turn around  against the Dolphins . For starters, Worthy is a candidate for some positive regression. He has converted only 11% of all air yards into completed air yards, which is an incredibly low rate. And while Worthy isn't strictly a run-straight-downfield receiver, he does run go routes or deep fades at an above-average rate.

 The Dolphins have played more single-high coverage than every team but the Browns. That should give Patrick Mahomes a chance to connect with Worthy on at least one outside vertical route.

 
 

 

 Jihaad Campbell , LB, Philadelphia Eagles : 13 tackles, 2 tackles for loss

 Campbell is close to an every-play role in Philadelphia's defense, and his numbers against the run have been strong. He's in the 94th percentile in run stop win rate and third best in NFL Next Gen Stats' defensive stop rate (a similarly-named but different statistic).

 With Bears quarterback  Caleb Williams  out of this game ( hamstring ), Chicago could be even more run-heavy than usual. And that ought to present a ton of tackling opportunities for Campbell.

 

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Dontayvion Wicks , WR, Philadelphia Eagles (rostered in 37.5% of ESPN leagues) 

 Wicks has emerged as Philadelphia's No. 2 receiver with at least four targets and 12 fantasy points in back-to-back games. He caught 5 of 6 targets for 74 yards in Tennessee  last week, and he could see even more opportunities against Chicago since TE  Dallas Goedert is out with an MCL sprain . The Bears have allowed the ninth-most passing yards per game this season.

 
 

 C.J. Stroud , QB, Houston Texans (33.8%) 

 Stroud has scored at least 16 fantasy points in each of the first two weeks of the season, as he's surrounded by  Nico Collins , Dalton Schultz and David Montgomery . This week -- even without Collins (hamstring) -- Stroud has a favorable matchup against a Colts defense that has allowed the third-most fantasy points per game to quarterbacks. Managers dealing with injuries to Jaxson Dart or Jayden Daniels shouldn't overlook Stroud as a streamer.

 
 

 Adonai Mitchell , WR, New York Jets (28.4%) 

 Mitchell's role took a big step forward in Week 2, when he drew a team-high 12 targets while playing 82% of the snaps. He has clearly become a major part of the passing game behind Garrett Wilson and has the speed to create big plays. The Lions are tied with the Texans for the most fantasy points allowed per game to wide receivers, and their depleted secondary makes Mitchell an intriguing sleeper.

 

 
 

 Bowen predicts three touchdown scorers 
 

 Cam Skattebo , RB, New York Giants 

 Skattebo has seen at least 16 touches a game this season, so we know the volume will be there versus Tennessee on Sunday. Plus, he had two carries inside the 5-yard line in the Giants' Week 1 win over the Cowboys, scoring on a 3-yard run. The Titans' defense has allowed three rushing scores this season.

 
 

 Kenneth Walker III , RB, Kansas City Chiefs 

 Walker scored twice in the Chiefs' Week 1 win over the Broncos (one rushing, one receiving), plus he's averaging 23.5 carries and 4.5 receptions per game. Those are big numbers for someone who was part of a committee approach in Seattle. Let's take Walker to score Sunday versus a Dolphins defense that has already surrendered eight touchdowns.

 
 

 Jalen Coker , WR, Carolina Panthers 

 Coker has quickly emerged in Carolina's offense, catching 16 of 18 targets for 204 yards so far -- including two touchdowns in Week 1 against the Bears. The Panthers also like to get Coker the ball in scoring position. He already has targets on red zone throws from quarterback Bryce Young , and I expect more on Sunday in Cleveland .

 

 

 Solak makes four more predictions 
 

 Ravens WR Zay Flowers  will go for another 150 yards 

 The Ravens get the Cowboys in Rio de Janeiro  this week . While I can't speak for the field conditions at Maracanã Stadium, I can speak to a Cowboys secondary woefully lacking in speed and man coverage ability. Flowers is the clear focal point of the Ravens' passing attack, and he should get plenty of free access targets Sunday. He got 150 yards in the first half of Week 1 before injuring his hamstring , which caused him to miss Week 2. Can Flowers knock on the door of 200 in Week 3?

 
 

 

 Jets QB Geno Smith  will throw three TD passes 

 He has only one through two games, as the Jets have largely been a run-heavy team and happy to play for field goals. Against the Lions' defense in a dome? I think we'll see a vintage Geno game. Plus, the Jets will likely spread the field out a little more given the absence of TE Mason Taylor  (thumb) and the weak spots at the Lions CBs.

 
 

 Raiders-Saints will be the game of the week 

 There are a couple of good contenders in Patriots-Jaguars and Rams-Broncos . But I want to see the Saints put together a complete game on offense, and they face a stiff Raiders defense that has impressed with speed and pressure from their front seven. Quarterback  Kirk Cousins has made it work without tight end  Brock Bowers so far, but the Saints should present the toughest defense…

title: The unshakable bond between Aaron Glenn and Dan Campbell
summary: Aaron Glenn and Dan Campbell grew up playing and then coaching in the NFL. When Campbell made Glenn his DC, their bond was sealed.
full_text:
The 2005 Dallas Cowboys were an incubator for future NFL head coaches, with six assistants from Bill Parcells' staff and two players from his roster ascending to the highest level of the football coaching profession.

 The future coaches included an intense, long-in-the-tooth cornerback who played bigger than his 5-foot-9 frame and a hulking tight end who was biting kneecaps long before he spoke it into the NFL lexicon.

 "He was the guy that Bill Parcells used to use to piss somebody off, and there were a number of fights in practice because of him," Aaron Glenn, the corner, said of Dan Campbell, the tight end.

 Campbell and Glenn formed a strong bond that season together. They went from teammates in Dallas to assistant coaches with the New Orleans Saints to head coach-defensive coordinator with the Detroit Lions , enduring tough times and moments of sheer joy.

 Their relationship was built on a promise by Campbell, who vowed to Glenn that he'd be his defensive coordinator if he ever became a head coach. Campbell did so in 2021 when he took over in Detroit, where the two developed an even closer bond, and doubled down in their first year together, standing by his guy in the 2022 season when it would have been easy to fire him after a rough start.

 "One of the greatest days of my life was him getting the [ New York Jets ] job, and one of the worst days of my life was him getting that job because you know you're losing a little piece of you," Campbell said Friday. "That's what he meant to me and to us. So, that's hard."

 On Sunday, they will face each other for the first time as head coaches (both sitting at 1-1), with Glenn bringing the Jets to Ford Field -- his home from 2021 to 2024. And nearly 500 miles away, at his house in Saratoga Springs, New York, the legendary Parcells will watch with pride.

 "I always told them all that [coaching] is not for well-adjusted people, so I don't know why they would pick that profession," Parcells said with a hint of sarcasm, alluding to Campbell, Glenn and his many protégés. "But they're football guys. They love it. That's their game."

 

 

 No change for the better 

 Campbell knew changes needed to be made in 2022 when the Lions were off to a 1-6 start.

 Coming off a 32-27 loss to the Miami Dolphins , Detroit scored on all five of its first-half possessions and entered halftime with a comfortable 10-point lead. But Glenn's defense squandered it, leading to a fifth consecutive loss.

 To that point, Glenn's unit was allowing a league-high 32.1 points per game, causing him to face heavy criticism, including calls for the first-time defensive coordinator to be fired.

 But Campbell maintained faith in Glenn. And the defense gradually improved, which was instrumental in Detroit winning eight of its final 10 games where it allowed just 20.2 points per game throughout that stretch and narrowly missed the playoffs.

 "[It] helps when you have somebody that you have a tremendous amount of trust for," Campbell said Friday. "You've been through a lot with them as a player and as a coach, you know what they're made of, and he's really -- he looks different than me. I'm taller, I'm whatever. He's quicker. All these different things, man, but we're really the same. I mean we're so much the same. And he's the defensive version, I'm the offensive version. And so, he was my right-hand man."

 Detroit would make some major changes, including firing defensive backs coach Aubrey Pleasant, but Glenn remained. Campbell credits Glenn for being a huge part of rebuilding the Lions' organization to what it is today after spending hours together planning and strategizing on ways they could improve. Glenn helped set the foundation for the Lions' current streak of four consecutive winning seasons (a first in over 50 years), including a franchise-best 15 wins in 2024.

 "Our players know exactly what's coming in here [on Sunday] because the defensive coordinator was here for five years," Campbell said. "... This is going to be a knockout, 60-minute brawl."

 

 

 This looks familiar 

 It's déjà vu in Detroit two weeks into the 2026 season. After a 1-1 start during which Detroit's defense allowed 71 points and gave up 915 total yards, Campbell recalled those tough early moments with Glenn.

 This time, Campbell is hearing some of those same concerns aimed at current defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, whom Campbell continues to vouch for -- just like he did for Glenn in 2022.

 "I never second-guessed [Glenn]. And even during that period when we were going through it, we came into that year '22 with 'All right, this is what'll be best for our front. We're going to become more attack style and shoot gaps.' And even though that's something we didn't believe in necessarily ... we felt it was the right thing with what we had at the time and it proved to not be," Campbell recalled. "And all right, man, we get through basically the bye week, we start to shift and get back to what we do a little bit of.

 "I think that's important, to be able to identify, 'All right, let's make this correction. Let's try this. Let's tighten this up. Let's go back to this.' That's a sign of a good coach. And [Sheppard has] got that too, but that's why AG just, he checked all those boxes, and you've got to look through all the other stuff and really look at the substance behind it."

 Former No. 2 pick Aidan Hutchinson was a rookie on the 2022 team in Detroit that got off to a slow start. He still remembers how the defense was able to turn things around.

 "AG is such a leader of men for sure," Hutchinson said Wednesday, "and I think we all always trusted him to figure that out and I think the same as with Shepp ... he's cut from the same cloth.

 "Different coaching styles a little bit, but I think, yeah, that's the intention right now is all hands on deck."

 

 

 'That friendship will always last' 

 As assistants on Sean Payton's staff with the New Orleans Saints from 2016 to 2020, Campbell and Glenn spent hours talking defense. Looking back, Glenn suspects that maybe those long talks were informal job interviews.

 Glenn said it was an honor to serve as defensive coordinator, adding, "I was the first guy he hired and it took -- I don't know -- maybe a week before we hired anybody else, and we just sat in my office, and we talked football, and how we were going to change this program around. Those things will always stick with me because the things that we talked about, we actually did, and Detroit actually ended up being exactly where they are now."

 Since taking over the Jets last year, Glenn has made references to Campbell, and how his former boss gave him occasional head coaching responsibilities -- i.e. creating the Lions' practice scripts and allowing him to address the entire team, not just the defense. Glenn believes those learning moments helped prepare him for his current position.

 "That friendship," Glenn said, "will always last."

 Naturally, Glenn's goal is to create a Detroit-like turnaround, which took considerable patience by Lions ownership. Under Campbell, the Lions started 4-19-1 before that midseason flip in 2022.

 In New York, Glenn's record is 4-15, triggering intense criticism. The slow start hasn't dented his confidence. After all, he lived it in Detroit, where his defensive schemes combined with Campbell's leadership and motivational fury to change the perception of the franchise.

 "They just fed off each other," said Jets wide receiver Tim Patrick , who played for the Lions in 2024. "Dan was the vocal part about it, but AG's energy carried the same thing Dan was speaking and they were just one."

 The best example of the synergy, Patrick said, was their pep talks before a Week 14 (Thursday night) game against the Green Bay Packers . In a now-celebrated speech, a fiery Campbell vowed to be aggressive with his playcalling and challenged the offense to compensate for an injury-riddled defense. Chiming in, Glenn…

title: How to bet Rams-Broncos on 'SNF': Analysis, tips and favorite plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet Rams-Broncos on "Sunday Night Football."
full_text:
Both teams rebounded from a tough Week 1 to look more like themselves last week.

 Matthew Stafford threw four touchdowns and recorded a 76 QBR as the  Los Angeles Rams beat the New York Giants  last week -- even without Puka Nacua and Myles Garrett . And Aaron Donald made his presence felt on defense, with a 30% pass rush win rate at defensive tackle that ranked sixth best at the position in Week 2. Even when not at full strength, this Rams team is mighty dangerous.

 

 And Denver showed that its disjointed Week 1 loss to Kansas City might have been a fluke by beating Jacksonville 20-13. The critical matchup here, of course, is the Rams offense against the vaunted Broncos defense.

 Will Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss fare better against Davante Adams than the Giants secondary did (my take: almost unequivocally, yes). And is the Rams running game where it has the advantage in this contest, against a Broncos unit that ranks last (!) in EPA allowed per opponent designed run?

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 
 My first guess was that, at 2.5-point favorites, the market was essentially writing off the Rams' Week 1 loss as a jet lag-inspired fluke. But then I checked ESPN's Football Power Index, and it's even more bullish on Los Angeles in this contest, favoring the Rams by 3.9 points.

 

 Part of that is because the Broncos, despite coming oh-so-close to the Super Bowl last year, didn't get that much respect from the model in the preseason (which means the betting market didn't give that much respect to Denver, either, since FPI's preseason ratings are largely driven by the betting market).

 Plus, while both of these teams suffered a blowout loss in Week 1, they are not equal: FPI believes the Rams lost to the best team in football (in San Francisco) while the Broncos were beaten by the fifth-best team in the Chiefs, who the model considers almost a field goal worse than the 49ers.

 I'm not betting the spread here, but if I were I would lean Los Angeles.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 Bo Nix rushing yards UNDER 17.5 (-111) 

 Ben Solak: Only one scramble through two games for Nix in 2026, which is notable, as Nix was scrambling 2.3 times per game in 2025. It doesn't seem to be related to the ankle injury -- he's moving just fine -- so my theory is that it's related to the new Davis Webb offensive approach. Either the Broncos brass has stressed upon him the importance of putting the ball in play, or Nix is more comfortable with the playcalls as they're given to him and is less likely to cut bait to tuck and go.

 Whatever it is, I'll take his under on his rushing yards against the Rams. With the litany of RB injuries the Broncos have, I think the Rams will be willing to play Nix's keeps on read-option a little more aggressively. I also expect the Rams to be a heavy zone team in this game despite the shift to man coverage in Week 2. Nix has historically been a much shakier passer against zone than man coverage. Zone coverage allows defenders to keep their eyes on scrambling quarterbacks, which limits yardage on the hoof.

 

 Jaylen Waddle receiving yards OVER 55.5 (-113) 

 Pam Maldonado: Waddle looks like Denver's clearest path to attack this Rams defense. Last week at home, Waddle drew 10 targets, caught eight passes and accounted for more than half of the team's air yards. This matchup fits that setup. The Rams have leaned heavily on man coverage. Waddle's speed makes him dangerous when defenders have to chase him across the field. Denver can also use quick throws to neutralize the Rams' pressure and get Waddle the ball in space. One explosive catch, paired with similar volume, can comfortably take him over his yardage prop.

 Terrance Ferguson 7-plus receptions (+552) 

 Walder: I was all the way in on Ferguson in fantasy in the preseason. And whatever chips I have left to push I'm sending in. The theory before the year was that if Puka Nacua or Davante Adams were out and if Ferguson could move past Colby Parkinson on the depth chart (or the Rams play enough two-tight end sets for it to not matter) then he would become the second-best receiving option on a lucrative offense. It was a good theory, but a few weeks ago it was just that: a theory. Now: we've seen it in action. Last week with Nacua out, Ferguson caught six passes, including a touchdown. I don't see any reason why the role should shrink assuming Nacua is out again. The opportunity is ripe for a right-tail, high-upside bet to hit.

title: 'Growing pains': What's going on with the Chargers' offense?
summary: Is the Chargers' offense too complicated for the team? What's going wrong with McDaniels' scheme in L.A.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- Quarterback  Justin Herbert furiously slammed his hands on the SoFi Stadium turf. He yelled as he stood up. Yelled as he began walking. Turned around and yelled some more. In the background, wide receiver  Tre' Harris  lay with his head buried in the turf.

 Just a moment before, the Chargers failed to convert on third down in the third quarter of their Week 2 loss to the Raiders, with the play failing basically before it even started. Harris came in motion as the play clock wound down on third-and-inches with Herbert in the shotgun, but as center Jake Slaughter snapped the ball, it hit Harris in the leg.

 Herbert jumped on the ball, and what followed was as intense of an outburst as he has had during a game in his seven-year career.

 

 The moment was a microcosm for the Chargers' 2026 season through two weeks: an offense seemingly too complicated for this team and a quarterback who appears as frustrated as he ever has been in a season that's trending toward being another year where success remains a hypothetical. The offense will look to bounce back this Sunday against the Buffalo Bills ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ).

 "Growing pains," coach Jim Harbaugh said. "Yeah, we got some growing pains."

 "We're not standing on business in the least," offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel said.

 McDaniel was the proverbial crown jewel of the Chargers' offseason.

 After two seasons of middling offensive play, Harbaugh fired  Greg Roman, the only offensive coordinator he had worked with in two stints in the NFL, following the Chargers'  16-3 wild-card round loss to the  New England Patriots .

 Fired in January  after four seasons as the coach of the  Miami Dolphins , McDaniel was still widely considered the top candidate available after the season. He's one of the most respected offensive minds in the NFL and chose to join the Chargers for the chance to work with Herbert and learn from Harbaugh.

 

 General manager Joe Hortiz spent the offseason retooling the team's offense to suit McDaniel's vision, which needed a different type of player for his wide zone scheme.

 McDaniel put up "wanted" posters for players he deemed essential, running back Keaton Mitchell and fullback Alec Ingold among them; Hortiz signed both. He added right guard Cole Strange , who worked with McDaniel when he coached the Dolphins, and drafted speedy wide receiver Brenen Thompson , partly at McDaniel's request.

 Players and coaches were equally excited about the offense's potential in the offseason. McDaniel promised "career highs across the board" for all the wide receivers.

 Instead, the Chargers had six fumbles versus the Raiders. Offensive tackle  Joe Alt  had three false starts. And Herbert didn't complete a pass of 20 air yards.

 "I think I can just plain and simply say that it's below our expectations," McDaniel said. "I know it's below a lot of people's expectations as well."

 Amid the struggles, McDaniel said that Herbert has blamed himself, which McDaniel doesn't believe is fair. He said the two of them have begun meeting more frequently and grown closer than they've ever been over the past two weeks.

 "It can be a lonely world as a starting quarterback," he said "... It can be lonely as a playcaller or an offensive coordinator. And the only way to approach it is that you're not alone."

 In the locker room after the loss to the Raiders, there was a mix of confusion and frustration. One team source told ESPN that the offense's poor execution doesn't make any sense because of how they practiced all summer. "We're making OTA mistakes," he said.

 

 Herbert's outburst on the third down was a reflection of the poor execution. If the play had continued without the fumble, an open running lane was forming on the left side of the line of scrimmage for  Omarion Hampton  to run through with Harris as a lead blocker. Mistakes caused the play to fail.

 And yet that poses a different question: Why was the playcall so complex in the first place? It was third-and-inches. The quarterback is 6-foot-6; the running back is a 220-pound, former first-round pick. It would seem that a sneak or under-center run would have done the trick.

 The complexity -- or the overcomplication even -- of this offense appears to be stumping the Chargers two weeks in. But Herbert rejected that theory.

 "I think every NFL offense is a complicated one," he said. "But I think it's just on us to be studying our stuff, making sure that we're ready to go."

 McDaniel said he has considered simplifying things as he gets to learn the players but is wary of overcorrecting.

 "Of course I consider [it]. I consider pretty much everything," he said. " What's important for my position is that if I'm saying not to overreact either way, good or bad.

 "What I know how to do is evolve. And so I think it's kind of lazy to just say, 'OK, there's the result. Not good. Let's do the opposite.' That's not why I'm here. That being said, you don't just point a finger and say, 'Well, it worked before.' So I think all of that is being taken under consideration."

 Nevertheless, the Chargers' offense has never looked this disjointed in the Harbaugh era.

 When comparing L.A.'s opening two games in the past two seasons under Roman with McDaniel's first two games, Roman's offense had far better numbers across the board, most notably a 75.82 offensive efficiency for Weeks 1 and 2 in 2025 (10th highest in the NFL) versus McDaniel's 17.97 offensive efficiency in 2026 (29th).

 Roman's scheme was simpler than McDaniel's, an approach Roman was criticized for. McDaniel uses pre-snap motion (74.1%) far more than Roman did last season (59.2%).

 Still, it has been an uncharacteristically bad start from a McDaniel offense, too.

 The Chargers' five turnovers are the most by a McDaniel offense through its first two games. Los Angeles' seven fumbles are its most through the first two games since at least 2000 and the most by a McDaniel offense.

 "We know we got to get better at a lot of different things and got to get better quick," Harris said.

 Even with the discouraging stats, the Chargers believe there are no fundamental issues with McDaniel's scheme. When they watch the film, they grow frustrated with the mistakes they are making that they say they don't see in practice. They'll get a chance to prove themselves this Sunday.

 "There are a lot of plays that we left out there," Herbert said. "I think it's promising to see all the plays that we could have made and how close we are."

title: How has Nakobe Dean reshaped the Raiders' defense?
summary: Nakobe Dean has stepped up in a big way to lead the Raiders' defense through two weeks.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. --  Nakobe Dean 's impact on the Las Vegas Raiders ' defense could be summarized by one play in the Week 2 win over the Los Angeles Chargers .

 The Raiders led 17-14 in the fourth quarter and needed to stop the Chargers from converting on third-and-2 from the 28-yard line. Quarterback Justin Herbert handed the ball off to second-year running back Omarion Hampton , hoping he could convert the short-yardage situation. Dean had a different plan.

 Dean maneuvered from the B-gap to the A-gap and met Hampton face-to-face before tackling him for no gain, forcing the Chargers to punt.

 

 Dean's performances through his first two weeks with the Raiders have been filled with clutch moments. He has made plays all over the field, racking up 15 tackles, 1.5 sacks, four pressures and a pair of forced fumbles.

 Over the offseason, the Raiders signed Dean to a three-year, $36 million deal. So far, it was money well spent.

 "He's been the glue to our defense," safety Jeremy Chinn told ESPN. "It's crazy how much a linebacker in the middle of the field can make such a difference in the back end and front end."

 Dean came to Las Vegas after four injury-riddled seasons with the  Philadelphia Eagles , who selected him in the third round of the 2022 draft. Dean played in at least 15 games only twice with the Eagles. But when he was on the field, Dean was effective. He compiled 226 tackles, 7.5 sacks, three forced fumbles and 19 tackles for loss in 47 games (27 starts).

 Las Vegas might have to give credit to Dean's intuition for landing one of the top off-ball linebackers in free agency. After the 2025 season, Dean had a competitive offer from the Dallas Cowboys  along with the Raiders.

 However, Dean thought about and prayed on both offers and ultimately, he couldn't go against his gut, which told him Las Vegas was the right fit.

 Dean and fellow teammate Quay Walker have reshaped the Raiders' inside linebacker room. Last year, Las Vegas filled the room with veterans who were past their prime and signed to one-year deals. The production was inconsistent.

 The Raiders took a new approach with Dean and Walker, both of whom are in the prime of their respective careers. And even though defensive coordinator Rob Leonard has had a strong start as a playcaller, Dean and Walker have been vital for the unit's ability to operate efficiently.

 

 Dean, in particular, has added much-needed support in the passing game. In six pass-rush snaps, Dean recorded a pressure rate of 66.7% and three quarterback hits. He recorded three pressures against the Chargers.

 As a whole, the Raiders have a league-leading sack total (eight) while ranked fifth in pressures (41) and first in pressure rate (50%). Of course, edge rusher Maxx Crosby has played a major role, but Dean has been much-needed support. Similar to Walker, Dean can line up in multiple spots up front. He has played 71 defensive snaps at inside linebacker, 12 at defensive tackle and 16 at outside linebacker.

 "You have guys that can consistently win one-on-one [matchups] or be able to disguise. It's huge for a defense," defensive tackle Thomas Booker IV told ESPN. "When you got guys getting home from blitzes and pressures, it makes everybody else's job easier. So it's great to have those two guys behind us."

 Dean has been just as impactful in stopping the run. He has collected 11 run tackles and two run stuffs. Dean has played in 120 defensive snaps (97%), and the Raiders have allowed 3.7 rushing yards per attempt when he is on the field. However, they have given up 11 yards per carry whenever he is on the sidelines.

 Las Vegas is 8th in total yards allowed per game (284.5), 14th in rushing yards allowed per game (100.5), but first in defensive rush total EPA (17.71).

 

 Dean's leadership has been invaluable. He is responsible for lining his teammates up and making sure everyone is on the same page. Dean's most important trait is his winning pedigree, which is why the Raiders were attracted to him in free agency.

 Dean won a national title during his final season in college at Georgia in 2021. His best season in Philadelphia was 2024, when he and the Eagles ultimately won a Super Bowl over the Kansas City Chiefs .

 His winning mentality has been essential to the Raiders' first 2-0 start since 2021. Another defining moment in the Raiders' matchup against the Chargers came late in the fourth quarter when Dean punched the ball out of Hampton's arm, resulting in a recovery from Chinn to help them secure the win.

 "He's a dog," Crosby said. "...You could rely on him in the biggest moments, and he's been playing his ass off."

title: Patriots need rookie LB Gabe Jacas to fill big shoes on defense
summary: The second-round pick has made impact plays over the first two weeks and will start vs. the Jaguars. Here's the latest on Jacas and other notes on the Patriots.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Jacas' motor: The short-handed Patriots defense is likely to turn to rookie outside linebacker Gabe Jacas as a starter in Sunday's road game against the Jacksonville Jaguars (1 p.m. ET, CBS), which might have been a concern a couple of weeks ago. But the second-round pick from Illinois has been one of the team's early-season surprises, which had Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers praising his relentlessness as the conversation surrounding Jacas has shifted as quickly as he darts to the football.

 Jacas, 22, has a motor-always-runs-hot play style. It has contributed to the Patriots (1-1) allowing just 16 points, helped him break the NFL's longest QB streak without an interception by recording the first pick against Rodgers since Week 10 of last season, and will be a key against Trevor Lawrence & Co. in Jacksonville with starting outside linebacker Dre'Mont Jones (shoulder) ailing.

 "That really came from when I started wrestling -- having that relentless mindset to not be denied," said Jacas, who was a two-time state championship grappler in high school.

 "And also having my brother [Khaliq] as a coach. He coached me that at an early age -- always run to the football, always having that motor. You never know what can happen if you run to the ball. Ever since then, running to the ball has been something that I do adamantly -- just like last game, stuff like that happens."

 

 Coach Mike Vrabel highlighted Jacas' hustle interception as an example of his improvement and willingness to take coaching.

 When defending a prior similar slip screen, Jacas ran to the quarterback and jumped in the air. Vrabel and outside linebackers coach Mike Smith told him the more effective approach is to put his foot in the ground, retrace and run to the football -- which is what he did against Rodgers.

 In addition, Vrabel spotlighted Jacas' strong play to tie up Steelers left tackle Troy Fautanu (2024 first-round pick), which freed up looping linebacker Christian Elliss for a crunching sack of Rodgers that was heard across the NFL.

 That Jacas would be involved in so many impact plays felt like a longshot a few weeks ago. He missed the entire spring after undergoing a knee procedure, which contributed to a contract impasse that led to him not signing his deal until a couple days into training camp.

 Then he was playing catch-up, which showed throughout the preseason when his aggressiveness had him out of position multiple times. But he had 19 snaps in the season-opening loss at Seattle (three tackles, sack), then saw a major uptick in playing time last week against the Steelers (49 snaps, 2 tackles, INT).

 Smith, the outside linebackers coach, said Jacas has benefited from the transition from the preseason to more game-planning in the regular season. He has consistently expressed his belief in Jacas, whose pass rush win rate of 8% shows there's still room for improvement, calling him "meaner than a wet mule."

 Jacas is studious, too.

 "Gabe is that guy you can just tell he loves football -- the questions he asks, him needing to get an understanding of all the plays and how to do things right and how to get better," second-year starting outside linebacker Elijah Ponder said. "He pays attention to detail and he's ready to learn, he's very coachable. I can't wait to see what his future holds."

 

 As for the immediate future, Jacas said he is excited to return to Florida for Sunday's game, albeit well north of where he grew up in Fort Pierce. He is expecting to have a large contingent of family and friends in attendance, which includes his high school wrestling coach Pat Seidel, mother Paula Henry and siblings -- including his oldest brother Khaliq.

 Having Khaliq in attendance for the second week in a row has added meaning of Jacas, who explained that Khaliq tutored him at Fort Pierce High School after finishing his playing career at Florida International in 2019.

 "I was a sophomore going into my junior year and he wanted to help me and coach me," Jacas said. "At first, it was more so volunteering, then he took over as D-line coach. Ever since then, he coached me for two years. I have a lot to give thanks to him for."

 So, too, do the Patriots, because they are now relying on Jacas quicker than anticipated.

 2. Injury comparison: The Patriots have placed 16 players on injured reserve (including the injury settlement to seventh-round pick Jam Miller ) in the 2026 league year, with starting right guard Mike Onwenu (ankle) and reserve safety Dell Pettus (ankle) going on the list in back-to-back days last week, and then outside linebacker Quintayvious Hutchins (knee) landing there Friday. In 2025, the Patriots placed 16 players on IR the entire season.  

 3. Maye check-in: One of the themes for Patriots quarterback Drake Maye through the first two games is that defenses are testing his willingness to be patient and drive the ball down the field -- sometimes playing a Cover 6 scheme with two deep safeties to take away the deep ball. Maye acknowledged he lost patience in the season opener when he threw three fourth-quarter interceptions, and quarterbacks coach Ashton Grant shared his view that Maye "settled down a little bit" in Week 2 against the Steelers.

 "Hopefully we can build off it," Grant said.

 4. Wilson rebound?: One way to help Maye is a sturdier interior of the pocket in pass protection. Center Jared Wilson , the 2025 third-round pick out of Georgia, is coming off a game that Vrabel said wasn't one of his best performances, adding: "I think he can protect better. I know he can protect better. I've seen him protect better."

 The Patriots also had to turn to veteran Greg Van Roten at right guard after Onwenu broke his right ankle, and he was also knocking off some rust. Vrabel said Van Roten is in line to start at that spot Sunday against the Jaguars.

 5. Lomu's impression: First-round draft pick Caleb Lomu , who grew up in Gilbert, Arizona, and attended Utah, talked about his "bests" and "worsts" of acclimating to New England:

 
 Best : "When you're in Boston, not including the driving, the people are amazing. The food is great; Mastro's has been a top restaurant. There's so many things to do. It's such a clean city, too, which I love. You really feel that everyone is a fan of the Patriots; they're coming up to you, super polite. I love how involved everyone is with the team, which makes it such a cool atmosphere." 
 Worst: "Just last week, I have to go get my wife from Logan [Airport] and it said 40 minutes. But then I get to the tunnel where you are going under water, and it ended up taking an hour, 10 minutes to get there. Which is the worst it's ever been. Then it took another hour, 10 minutes to get back. So I'd say that's the worst part of my experience so far in Boston -- the traffic." 
 
 

 6. Ramirez's reaction: Recently signed Patriots outside linebacker Jose Ramirez had been cut by the Eagles on Aug. 30, and after clearing waivers the following day, he said he had a flight to return home that night. That's when he heard from Patriots scouting administration coordinator Courtney Weiner, who he said apologized for the timing of booking a 6 a.m. flight the next morning for him to come join New England's practice squad.

 The soft-spoken Ramirez described his reaction this way: After not breaking through with the Buccaneers (2023-2024), playing for the Hamilton Tiger-Cats of the CFL in 2025 and getting caught in a numbers crunch with the Eagles this spring, he would have walked to Foxborough if that's what was asked of him.

 While injuries in front of him opened his path to a roster spot in New England, coaches also said Ramirez (four career NFL games played) was exemplary on the scout team in recent weeks.
